At every point of $\partial\Omega_v$ the vacuum region $\Omega_v$ is locally exactly the one-sided subgraph of a $C^k$ graph. Let $x\in\partial\Omega$. Use the chart of [F4] for $\Omega$ at $x$ and let $\rho:=\rho_x>0$ [step 1.1]; replacing $W$ by the open set $W\cap B(x,\rho/2)$ preserves the chart identity [F4] and makes $W\cap K=\varnothing$, so $\Omega_v\cap W=\Omega\cap W$ and $R(\Omega_v\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{s<h(y)\}$. Let $x\in\partial D_j$. Use the chart of [F4] for $D_j$ at $x$, and replace $W$ by an open ball about $x$ contained in $\Omega$ and avoiding $\bigcup_{i\ne j}\overline{D_i}$; this keeps the chart identity [F4] and gives $\Omega_v\cap W=W\setminus\overline{D_j}$, whose image is $R(W)\cap\{s>h(y)\}$: points with $s<h(y)$ lie in $D_j$, points with $s=h(y)$ lie on $\partial D_j$ [F4, F5]. Put $\rho_0(y,s):=(y,-s)$ and $R_0:=\rho_0\circ R$, $h_0:=-h$; then $R_0$ is a rigid motion, $h_0\in C^k$, and $R_0(\Omega_v\cap W)=R_0(W)\cap\{s<h_0(y)\}$ [F7, F8].
The boundary pieces of [step 2.2] are the compact embedded $C^k$ hypersurfaces of the boundary lemma, and they are pairwise disjoint with nonempty compact pieces; this is (b).

$\Omega_v$ is a bounded $C^k$ domain: it is nonempty [step 2.1], bounded and open [step 1.1], and by [step 2.2] every boundary point is treated by one of the two local charts of [step 3.1], each exhibiting $\Omega_v$ locally as the one-sided subgraph of a $C^k$ function over an open ball after a rigid motion [F4, F8]. This is (a).

The normals. In the $\partial\Omega$ case of [step 3.1] the chart data for $\Omega_v$ and for $\Omega$ are identical, so the prescribed outward normal of $\Omega_v$, computed by the formula of [F4], equals that of $\Omega$ at every point of $\partial\Omega$. In the $\partial D_j$ case, the chart of $\Omega_v$ is $R_0=\rho_0\circ R$ with graph $h_0=-h$; the orthogonal part of $R_0$ is $\rho_0Q$, whose inverse is $Q^{\mathsf T}\rho_0$, so [F4] gives the vacuum normal $(Q^{\mathsf T}\rho_0)(-Dh_0(y),1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh_0(y)|^2}=(Q^{\mathsf T}\rho_0)(Dh(y),1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}$, and since $\rho_0(Dh,1)=(Dh,-1)=-(-Dh,1)$ this equals $-Q^{\mathsf T}(-Dh(y),1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh(y)|^2}$, the negative of the prescribed outward normal of $D_j$ [F4, F8]. This is (c).

Connected collars and patches. Fix one of the charts of [step 3.1], shrinking its neighborhood to be bounded first. Write $R$ for its rigid motion, $W$ for its domain, $h$ for its graph function and $B''$ for the set of parameters $y$ with $(y,h(y))\in R(W)$, an open subset of $B$ containing the parameter of the distinguished boundary point. Choose a ball $B_1$ with $\overline{B_1}\subseteq B''$; the compact graph set $G:=\{(y,h(y)):y\in\overline{B_1}\}\subseteq R(W)$ ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]], [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]) is disjoint from the closed set $\mathbb R^3\setminus R(W)$, the function $z\mapsto d(z,\mathbb R^3\setminus R(W))$ is positive and continuous on $G$ (its Lipschitz constant is at most one by the triangle inequality), hence has a positive minimum $\delta$ by [F3]. Its complement is nonempty because $W$ is bounded. By continuity of $h$ at the parameter $y_x$ of the distinguished point choose a ball $B_1'\subseteq B_1$ around $y_x$ with $|h(y)-h(y_x)|\le\delta/4$ for $y\in B_1'$ [F8]. In the inner case the region $T:=\{(y,s):y\in B_1',\ h(y)<s<h(y)+\delta\}$ is contained in $R(W)$ (every point of $T$ is within $\delta$ of its graph point, which lies in $G$) and in $\{s>h(y)\}$, so $R^{-1}(T)\subseteq\Omega_v\cap W$; in the outer case the same holds for $T:=\{(y,s):y\in B_1',\ h(y)-\delta<s<h(y)\}$ and $\{s<h(y)\}$, by the descriptions of [step 3.1]. The set $T$ is polygonally connected by [F6], hence connected, so $N:=R^{-1}(T)$ is connected as its continuous image [F7]; moreover $N$ accumulates at every point $X(y)$ of the patch $P:=X(B_1')\subseteq\partial\Omega_v$, since the points $(y,h(y)\pm\varepsilon)$ with $0<\varepsilon<\delta$ lie in $T$ and converge to $(y,h(y))$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.
Each connected component of the open set $\Omega_v$ is open in $\mathbb R^3$ and polygonally connected [F9]; in particular every component is open.

Each patch is incident to exactly one component. The connected nonempty collar $N$ of step 4.3 lies in one component $U$ of $\Omega_v$ [F9]. For $z=X(y_0)\in P$, continuity of $h$ and openness of $B_1'$ give a ball $B(z,r)$ so small that its chart coordinates satisfy $y\in B_1'$ and $|s-h(y)|<\delta$, and that $B(z,r)\subset W$. By step 3.1 the vacuum portion of this ball lies in the one-sided collar, hence $B(z,r)\cap\Omega_v\subset N\subset U$. If $z\in\partial U_1$ for another component, the ball meets $U_1$ by [F2], so $U_1$ meets $N$ and equals $U$ by [F9]. Conversely, every $z\in P$ is in $\partial U$ because the collar accumulates there and $z\notin\Omega_v$. Thus every point of $P$ is incident to exactly $U$.

Every component is incident to a patch. Let $U$ be a component of $\Omega_v$. It is nonempty, open and bounded, so $\partial U\ne\varnothing$: otherwise $\overline U=U$, making $U$ a nonempty clopen proper subset of the connected space $\mathbb R^3$ (proper since $U$ is bounded), contradicting [F10]. Also $\partial U\subseteq\partial\Omega_v$: if $x\in\partial U$ then $x\in\overline U\subseteq\overline{\Omega_v}$ and $x\notin\Omega_v$, because $\Omega_v$ is open and $x$ lies neither in the open set $U$ nor in its open complement in $\Omega_v$ [F2, F9]. By [step 2.2] and [step 3.2] every point of $\partial\Omega_v$ lies on one of the finitely many boundary pieces, and the patches of the kind constructed in [step 4.3] cover each piece; so some such patch $P$ meets $\partial U$, and [step 5.2] identifies $U$ as the unique component incident to $P$.

Finitely many components. The patches of the kind constructed in [step 4.3], for all boundary points, cover $\partial\Omega_v$ [step 6.1], and $\partial\Omega_v$ is compact [step 3.2]; hence finitely many of them already cover $\partial\Omega_v$. Each determines exactly one component [step 5.2], and every component is determined by one of them [step 6.1]; therefore the components of $\Omega_v$ are among these finitely many, so $\Omega_v$ has finitely many connected components.

Each component is a bounded $C^k$ domain with the stated boundary. Let $U$ be a component of $\Omega_v$ and let $P$ be a patch incident to $U$ [step 6.1]. The local description of [step 3.1] shows that, in the chart of $P$, $U$ coincides with the one-sided region described there, hence is locally exactly the one-sided subgraph of the $C^k$ function $h$ (outer case) or of the reflected $C^k$ function $h_0=-h$ (inner case) over a ball [F4, F8, step 3.1, step 5.2]. So $U$ is a bounded $C^k$ domain: it is open [step 5.1], bounded (a subset of bounded $\Omega_v$) and nonempty [F9]. Every point of a patch incident to $U$ is a boundary point of $U$ (it lies in $\partial\Omega_v$ and in the closure of the collar $N\subseteq U$ [step 4.3, step 5.2]), and conversely every boundary point of $U$ lies in a patch incident to $U$ [step 6.1]; hence $\partial U$ equals the union of those patches in a finite covering that are incident to $U$. It is compact because it is closed in $\mathbb R^3$ [F2] and contained in the compact $\partial\Omega_v$ [step 3.2], by [F1]. Finally, let $C$ be a connected component of $\partial\Omega_v$; the assignment to $x\in C$ of the component of $\Omega_v$ incident to a patch containing $x$ takes values in a finite set and is locally constant on $C$ (near a point of a patch it is given by the single component of that patch [step 5.2]), so it is constant on the connected set $C$ [F10]; hence each boundary component of $\partial\Omega_v$ is incident to exactly one component of $\Omega_v$, and $\partial U$ is a union of such boundary components. The normal formulas of [step 4.2] apply verbatim to each piece of $\partial U$, since they are the same local charts. This is (d); connectedness of $\Omega_v$ itself is neither assumed nor asserted.

risk_review.notes: All thirteen steps checked against exact chart, compactness, component, continuity and extreme-value interfaces. K is compact and the m=0 branch never takes distance to the empty set. Outer and inner boundary identities use local one-sided graphs; reflection changes the side and the inverse matrix is Q^T rho0 throughout. The refuter sphere chart yields opposite e1 vectors for Q^T rho0 e3 and Q rho0 e3, confirming the false intermediate equality; restoring Q^T repairs it completely. Compact graph patches have positive collar width via distance to the nonempty closed complement. Each sufficiently small vacuum neighborhood lies in one connected collar, giving a unique incident component; a finite boundary cover gives finite vacuum components, and local constancy on boundary components gives the claimed restricted boundaries. Disconnected Omega and conductors with holes remain admitted. No statement or definition changes; consumer normal sign is preserved. AC_omega is carried but no stronger choice is spent.

boundaries.evidence: The conductor surface S is nonempty: the model has m>=1 bodies with nonempty boundaries ([F5]); the pointwise clause with sigma=0 at a point is the empty-flux sub-case handled in step 1.1.
Step 1.1 covers sigma=0 at a point: n.E_+=0 and n x E_+=0 force E_+=0 by [F6]; Q_j=0 corresponds to vanishing flux in step 3.1, and the zero field on the conductor side is used throughout.
A single connected component of S is treated in step 1.2, where the trace is constant with value V_j; one conductor body in clause (d) is the single-integral case of step 3.1.
Corner or edge degeneracy is excluded by the smooth-surface hypothesis; the vanishing tangential part n x E_+=0 of clause (a) is proved, not assumed, in step 1.1.
Step 1.2 uses continuity of the model potential at every point of the conductor closure to identify the trace directly with V_j; no offset-chart derivative limit is required.
AC_omega is declared for the surface and distribution interfaces and enters through [F2] and [F5] as used in step 1.1; the pointwise argument itself uses no further choice principle.

boundaries.reason: Clauses (a)-(d) are identities and constancy statements; the 'equivalently' in (a) is an algebraic rearrangement of the first identity proved in step 1.1, not an iff claim.
No converse of the boundary relations is asserted.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) as carried by the declared
distributional and surface source objects of [[def-em-weak-sources]]. In the
flat classical laboratory model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the positive
constants and SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]], adopt the following
additional physical assumption for models using the declared point or
stationary-sheet sources: the locally integrable field pair and the
volume-plus-singular source pair of [[def-em-weak-sources]](a)-(d) must satisfy
its solution predicate (e). Explicitly,

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$

are required in $\mathcal D'(U)$, meaning that all four residual pairings
defined there vanish for every compact smooth test. This is a physical adoption
of the classical vacuum idealisation in that source class, not a theorem about
sources and not a consequence of the original locally integrable source branch
of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. When the singular part vanishes, the adopted
identities coincide with that earlier weak branch.

Only source and field tuples satisfying these identities are models of this
postulate; the postulate does not assert existence for every prescribed source
pair, and compatibility conditions remain consequences to be checked. Sources
are the exact point and stationary-sheet types defined earlier, including their
properness or endpoint and tangential-current qualifications. No moving sheet,
line current, magnetic source, product of distributions, self-force,
regularisation, matter dynamics or material constitutive law is introduced.
This postulate reports no experiment or measurement and does not infer
empirical certainty from its mathematical formulation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the surface-measure interface inherited from [[def-em-surface-distribution]]
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory
region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\mathcal D'(U)$ be the space of
distributions on $U$ ([[def-distribution]],
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]); recall that the pairing
$\langle T,\psi\rangle$ is bilinear with no conjugation and that the
distributional partial derivatives are
$\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$
([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(a) [Fields as distributions] Locally integrable fields and source densities on
$U$ are identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

(b) [Point sources] Let $I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval,
let $z:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ trajectory whose graph map
$\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$ is proper into the open set $U$, and let $q\in\mathbb R$
(coulombs). By [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]],

$$\langle\rho_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}z'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$$

define distributions on $U$ with
$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=0$. If instead
$I_0=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the
absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite and both endpoint
events lie in $U$, the same formulas define distributions with

$$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=q\,\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\,\delta_{\gamma(b)}$$

([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); a finite-history point source
therefore contributes an endpoint term unless that term is included
explicitly, and the pairings above exclude it only by the stated properness or
endpoint hypotheses.

(c) [Stationary-sheet sources] Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded
$C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side
$\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]],
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]), and let
$\sigma:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous
with $K(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$; $\sigma$ carries C m$^{-2}$ and $K$ carries A m$^{-1}$ (a tangential surface current
density; the sheet is stationary). Then

$$\langle\rho_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_S\sigma(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_SK(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt$$

define distributions on $U$: for $\psi$ with compact support the inner
integrals are continuous in $t$ on a compact parameter interval and the
functionals are bounded by
$(\sup|\sigma\psi|)\,\mathrm{area}(S)\,\mathrm{length}$ of the time projection
of the support, and likewise in the vector case. A normal sheet current (one
with $K\cdot n\ne0$), a line current and a moving sheet are not source types of
this definition.

(d) [Unrestricted weak fields and optional interface branches] The general
field class for the solution predicate (e) consists of all locally integrable
pairs $(E,B)$ on $U$, also when the source has a stationary-sheet part. No
classical one-sided trace or off-sheet $C^1$ regularity is required to define
those four distributional pairings. Additional trace hypotheses are optional
hypotheses of interface and jump results, not admission requirements of the
general weak model.

For a pointwise classical jump branch, one may additionally assume that $E,B$
are $C^1$ off $S\times I$ and, around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side
is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of
the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder. These
joint one-sided extensions make the field traces and first spatial and
temporal derivatives continuous up to that side, locally uniformly on compact
cylinders.

For the broader weak-trace branch, retain spacetime $C^1$ regularity on
$(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$ and assume the original one-sided spatial
$C^1$ extensions at each time, with the explicit additional
conditions that the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the field traces are measurable and locally
integrable on $S\times I$ for $dS\,dt$. This branch supports sheet-distribution
and almost-everywhere jump identities; spatial continuity at each time gives
pointwise spatial identities for almost every time, and joint continuity of
the jump densities gives the further all-time upgrade. Separate spatial $C^1$
traces at each time alone do not imply that joint regularity or upgrade.
Whenever such traces exist, $[F]:=F_+-F_-$ denotes their jump in the chosen
normal convention.

(e) [Weak Maxwell equations with a distributional source pair] Let $E,B$ be a
field pair of class (d), let $\rho=\rho_v+\rho_s$ and $J=J_v+J_s$ be source
distributions on $U$ whose volume parts $\rho_v,J_v$ are locally integrable
volume densities with the charge and current quantity types of
[[def-em-sources]] (the weak predicate requires this stated
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ regularity, not the classical continuous-source
regularity) and whose singular parts $(\rho_s,J_s)$ are point sources as in (b)
or stationary-sheet sources as in (c), and let
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]. Say that $E,B$ satisfy the weak Maxwell equations
with the source pair $(\rho,J)$ when, for every
$\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, the four pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish, all derivatives being distributional derivatives of the regular
distributions of the fields and the source pairings being those of (b) and (c).
This clause defines a solution predicate. When the singular parts vanish, its
four identities are the same as the locally integrable weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. That earlier postulate explicitly excludes point
and sheet distributions and does not imply their physical adoption here;
adoption for the declared singular-source models is made separately, after
this definition. No physical field equation is deduced merely from defining
this predicate.

(f) [Scope] No product of two distributions is formed anywhere: the fields
occur only through their distributional derivatives paired with a test
function, and the source densities $\sigma,K$ occur only inside the ordinary
surface and time integrals of (b) and (c); products such as $\rho_sE$ or
$J_s\times B$ are not defined by this item. The definition asserts no existence
theorem for fields with singular sources, no conservation law (continuity for
these sources is proved separately where used) and no regularisation. Sources
that are not locally integrable and are not point or stationary-sheet sources,
moving sheets, line currents, and arbitrary products of distributions are
outside the definition.

Throughout, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the surface integral of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and the domains of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] are developed under that convention.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open. Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface ([[def-codimension-and-hypersurface]], [[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]): every $p\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^2\times\{0\})$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Such an $S$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, so the surface integral and the surface measure $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf 1_A\,dS$ of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]] apply; that measure is finite. The slice-chart definition has no manifold boundary; $S$ has no edge. If $S$ is empty, all surface functionals below are zero and the estimates are read separately without taking a supremum over the empty set.

A **two-sided presentation** of $S$ consists of a continuous unit normal field $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ together with sides: $n(x)$ is orthogonal to $S$ at $x$ in the sense that $\langle n(x),\gamma'(0)\rangle=0$ for every $C^1$ path $\gamma:(-1,1)\to S$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\lVert n(x)\rVert_2=1$; and $\Omega_-,\Omega_+\subseteq\Omega$ are open sets with

$$\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+,\qquad \Omega_-\cap\Omega_+=\varnothing,$$

such that for every $x\in S$ there is $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(x)>0$ with $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_+$ for all $0<s<\varepsilon$ and $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_-$ for all $-\varepsilon<s<0$. The normal $n$ points from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$; the orientation convention for normals is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

**The surface distribution $\delta_S$.** For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS,$$

where the right-hand side is the surface integral of the restriction of $\psi$ to $S$, taken in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; complex-valued $\psi$ are integrated componentwise in real and imaginary parts. For a continuous **density** $a:S\to\mathbb R$ define

$$a\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S a\,\psi\,dS .$$

Both are complex-linear functionals on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, and both are distributions: $\delta_S,a\delta_S\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[def-distribution]]).

**Jumps across $S$.** Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be a field that is of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately and has one-sided continuous traces: there are continuous maps $F_+,F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3$ with

$$F_+(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_+}}F(y),\qquad F_-(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_-}}F(y)$$

for every $x\in S$, the limits taken in $\mathbb R^3$. The **jump of $F$ across $S$** is the continuous map

$$[F]:=F_+-F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3 .$$

No continuity of $F$ across $S$ is assumed or implied; $F$ need not even be defined on $S$, and the two traces may differ.

### Well-definedness and finite order

*The surface functionals are distributions.* Fix a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ with the seminorm $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K|\psi|$ of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. Since $\psi$ vanishes outside $K$ and is continuous, $\sup_S|\psi|\le p_0(\psi)$; and $\int_S|a\psi|\,dS\le\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\sup_S|\psi|\,S(S)$ with $\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}<\infty$ by compactness of $S$ and continuity of $a$. Hence

$$|\delta_S(\psi)|\le S(S)\,p_0(\psi),\qquad |a\delta_S(\psi)|\le \lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\,S(S)\,p_0(\psi),$$

a finite-order estimate of order $0$ with constants independent of $K$; by the local finite-order characterization ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]) both functionals are distributions. This is the sense in which boundedness on the compact interface and finiteness of the surface measure give continuity of finite order. Linearity is immediate from linearity of the integral; the pairing is complex bilinear with no conjugation, as in [[def-distribution]].

*The field has locally integrable components.* The hypersurface $S$ is a Lebesgue-null set of $\mathbb R^3$: by the slice-chart property it is covered by finitely many compact pieces each of which is, in suitable $C^2$ coordinates, a graph over a compact subset of a coordinate plane, hence has content zero ([[thm-graph-of-continuous-function-on-a-compact-set-has-content-zero]]), and each piece has content zero in the ambient coordinates because it is the image under the $C^1$ chart inverse of a compact content-zero set ([[lem-c-one-images-of-content-zero-compact-sets-have-content-zero]]); a finite union of compact content-zero sets is compact and null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]), hence has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $S$ has content zero in the sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. Now $F$ is continuous on $\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$. For each $x\in S$, the two one-sided limits are finite; hence there is a neighbourhood $U_x$ of $x$ on which $|F|$ is bounded on each side (use the defining limit with tolerance $1$ for each of $F_+(x)$ and $F_-(x)$). Away from $S$, continuity also gives a neighbourhood with a finite bound at every point. For a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, these neighbourhoods cover $K$; take a finite subcover and the maximum of its finitely many bounds. This gives a finite $M_K$ such that $|F|\le M_K$ on $K\setminus S$. Extend $F$ by zero on the null closed set $S$; the extension is measurable because the two side restrictions are continuous, and

$$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le M_K\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

the contributions from $K\cap S$ being null. Thus the components of $F$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], and define a regular distribution; the trace condition is exactly what makes the boundary values $F_\pm$ well-defined continuous functions on $S$, so the jump $[F]$ is continuous and bounded on $S$.

### Conventions and exclusions

The sign convention is fixed by the normal: $n$ points from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, so $[F]=F_+-F_-$ is measured in the direction of $n$. This convention is used by the interface-derivative lemma on this page, where $\operatorname{div}F$ and $\operatorname{curl}F$ acquire the surface terms $n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S$ and $n\times[F]\,\delta_S$; reversing $n$ reverses the signs of both sides consistently. The definition assumes a fixed stationary interface $S$: no time dependence of $S$ is part of the data, and the stationary jump formulas are not asserted for moving interfaces. The density $a$ is continuous, so $a\delta_S$ is defined by the displayed integral; no product of two arbitrary distributions, and no product of $\delta_S$ with a merely locally integrable field, is defined here. The definition is stated under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ because the surface measure it invokes is; the positivity of the surface measure of nonempty open pieces of $S$, and the finite-order estimates above, are its only uses here.

Under the Countable Choice convention of the stated boundary and sheet-distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), adopt as a physical model of ideal electrostatic conductors, for the classical laboratory framework of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]: a **conductor configuration** consists of the following data, and every model of this postulate is required to satisfy the clauses below. No experiment is reported and no empirical value is inferred; this is an explicitly adopted equilibrium idealization together with its geometric and source conventions.

(a) [Geometry] a laboratory region $\Omega\times I$ with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ an arbitrary open ambient region, a finite family $D_1,\dots,D_m$ ($m\ge1$) of bounded $C^\infty$ domains with pairwise disjoint closures in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] with closures strictly inside $\Omega$ (the **conductor bodies**), the **conductor** $D:=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_m$, its **surface** $\partial D$, and the **vacuum region** $\Omega_v:=\Omega\setminus\overline D$. By [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]], $\partial D=\partial D_1\cup\cdots\cup\partial D_m$ is a disjoint union of compact embedded $C^\infty$ hypersurfaces. The vacuum $\Omega_v$ is open, and near each conductor surface it is locally the smooth exterior side of that conductor. No boundedness or regularity of the ambient boundary is inferred from openness. In the additional **bounded smooth ambient branch**, assume that $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^\infty$ domain; only then [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]] gives that $\Omega_v$ is a bounded $C^\infty$ domain with the specified outer/conductor boundary charts; we additionally require $\Omega_v$ to be connected (configurations whose vacuum region is separated by the conductors, for instance by an enclosing closed shell, are outside this model as formulated here).

(b) [Equilibrium and sources] the configuration is in the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] on the vacuum region: $B=0$, $J=0$, $E$ is the fixed-time electric field of [[def-em-fields]], the volume source density $\rho_v$ is a continuous real map on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ (C m$^{-3}$, [[def-em-sources]]) extended by zero to $D$; the **conductor charge is a stationary surface charge**, i.e. a continuous density $\sigma:\partial D\to\mathbb R$ (C m$^{-2}$) whose pairing with test functions is the stationary-sheet source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) with tangential current $K=0$ and $S=\partial D$; and the field pair $(E,0)$ together with the source pair $(\rho_v+\sigma\,\delta_{\partial D},\ 0)$ satisfies the adopted distributional vacuum Maxwell equations [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]]. Inside the conductor the field vanishes: $E\equiv0$ on $D$ (the **equilibrium condition**); equivalently the conductor interior is field-free and carries no volume charge.

(c) [Potential and equipotential convention] there is a function $\varphi\in C^0(\Omega)\cap C^2(\Omega_v)$ with $E=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\Omega_v$ and with $\varphi$ constant on each conductor body, $\varphi|_{D_j}\equiv V_j$ for real constants $V_j$ (volts, [[def-em-si-conventions]]); by continuity of $\varphi$ the trace of $\varphi$ on each $\partial D_j$ from the vacuum side equals $V_j$ as well. This is the single-function convention of an ideal conductor with no double layer: the model reads the same potential value on both sides of $\partial D_j$, while the normal component of $E$ may jump.

(d) [Data] a model is completed either by the component potentials $V_1,\dots,V_m$ together with the volume source $\rho_v$ and the data on $\partial\Omega$ where the laboratory region is bounded, or by the component total charges $Q_j:=\int_{\partial D_j}\sigma\,dS$ (C) together with those same ambient data. These are two declared data types; the postulate asserts neither that both data types are simultaneously specifiable nor that either is solvable for arbitrary data.

(e) [Scope] This is a static, frame-relative equilibrium idealization: it excludes transient finite-conductivity dynamics, relaxation to equilibrium, moving surface charge, electrode polarization and contact effects, and it is not derived from a microscopic matter model. It asserts no existence or uniqueness theorem (those are separate conditional results), no force, no energy, no radiation, no measurement and no apparatus realization; the value $V_j$ is a model parameter and the surface density $\sigma$ is an idealization variable determined by the equilibrium problem when it is solvable. The general open ambient branch retains compact conductor bodies in exterior configurations. Its additional bounded smooth ambient branch is distinct from the separately declared grounded-half-space and infinite parallel-plane idealizations, whose conductor bodies are themselves noncompact. Those examples retain the equilibrium/equipotential interpretation but their noncompact bodies and plane distributions are not instances of this compact-body configuration or its compact-sheet predicate. No arbitrary exterior solvability is asserted.

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units, constants and symbols of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and let $(\rho,J)$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$, all of class $C^1$ (with every additional derivative appearing below existing and continuous); $\partial_t$ is the partial time derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

(a) [Static regime] The **static (time-independent) electromagnetic regime** on $\Omega\times I$ is the requirement
$$\partial_tE=0,\qquad\partial_tB=0,\qquad\partial_t\rho=0,\qquad\partial_tJ=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

(b) [Pure electrostatics] The **pure electrostatic regime** is the static regime together with $J=0$ and $B=0$ on $\Omega\times I$.

(c) [Reduced equations] If the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds in the static regime, then the four Maxwell equations reduce to
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$$
pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied at each fixed time; in the pure electrostatic regime the reduction is exactly the pair $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$.

(d) [Fixed-time reading] In the static regime $E,B,\rho,J$ do not depend on $t$, so each is the pullback along $(y,t)\mapsto y$ of a single map on $\Omega$; this fixed-time reading (the spatial field or source) is the object analysed by the electrostatic statements of this page, and no other time dependence is introduced. The equations of (c) are equations between those spatial maps.

(e) [Static-to-distributional reading] Let fields $E,B$ and volume densities $\rho,J$ be locally integrable and time independent on $\Omega\times I$, and let $\Omega$ be open. Then, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the cited measure and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), the weak equations of the solution predicate of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e) for these time-independent objects hold if and only if the four spatial equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$; the passage between them is the integration in $t$ of the pairings against $C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ tests, justified by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] after identifying fields and densities with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). In particular a **stationary point charge** at $x_0\in\Omega$ with charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ is the point source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with constant trajectory $z(t)\equiv x_0$, whose pairing is $\psi\mapsto q\int_I\psi(x_0,t)\,dt$ and whose fixed-time reading is the spatial point source $\eta\mapsto q\eta(x_0)$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).

(f) [Conventions and scope] The regime is imposed in the one inertial frame of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; no claim is made that time independence survives a change of inertial description, and where a frame change is used the transformed fields must be rechecked. The static regime is an adopted idealization, not a dynamical stability theorem: static charged matter requires external support or an adopted equilibrium model. No equation is asserted here for singular sources beyond the dictionary of (e), and no empirical claim is made.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the interface and surface-measure definitions cited below
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory
region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]] and the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and source
fields of [[def-em-sources]].

Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a
chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side
$\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]]), and let
$\sigma:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous
with $K(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a tangential surface current
density). Let $E,B$ be locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$ and $C^1$ on
$(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$ with the following explicit joint one-sided
regularity: around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side is the restriction
of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of the corresponding
closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder. Thus the fields and their
first space and time derivatives extend continuously to that side of
$S\times I$, locally uniformly on compact cylinders, and let $\rho_v,J_v$ be
continuous on $(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$ and locally integrable on
$\Omega\times I$. Write $[F]=F_+-F_-$ for the jump of the one-sided traces of
such a field $F$.

Under the separate singular-source physical adoption
[[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], suppose that $E,B$ satisfy the weak
Maxwell equations with the source pair

$$\rho=\rho_v+\rho_S,\qquad J=J_v+J_S,$$

where $(\rho_S,J_S)$ is the stationary-sheet source of
[[def-em-weak-sources]](c) with densities $\sigma,K$ and the pairings there, in
the sense of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e), and where the volume parts
$\rho_v,J_v$ are identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Then, pointwise
on $S\times I$,

$$n\cdot[E]=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad n\times[B]=\mu_0K,\qquad n\cdot[B]=0,\qquad n\times[E]=0,$$

with the ordinary Euclidean inner and cross products of the one-sided traces
([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Equivalently, the surface current density is
$K=(\mu_0)^{-1}\,n\times[B]$ and the surface charge density is
$\sigma=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot[E]$.

The theorem assumes a stationary interface: the hypersurface $S$ and its
normal do not depend on $t$, so the one-sided $C^1$ traces also make
$\partial_tE$ and $\partial_tB$ locally bounded near $S$ and hence locally
integrable, contributing no delta terms. No magnetic surface charge or
magnetic surface current is present in the sources, and correspondingly the
last two identities assert the absence of magnetic sheet delta terms. A moving
interface, a normal sheet current, or a sheet whose support changes with time
is outside this statement and would require additional terms.

[General weak-trace branch] The weak Maxwell framework continues to allow the
full locally integrable field and source class, without asserting undefined
classical trace values. If instead of the joint extension condition the fields
have the original one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time, assume in
addition that their piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega\times I)$ and that their one-sided field traces are
measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ with respect to $dS\,dt$.
The one-sided traces are then locally integrable densities on the sheet, so
the four pairings
$$\int_I\int_S\bigl(n\cdot[E]-\sigma/\varepsilon_0\bigr)\psi\,dS\,dt,\quad\int_I\int_S(n\cdot[B])\psi\,dS\,dt,\quad\int_I\int_S(n\times[E])\psi\,dS\,dt,\quad\int_I\int_S\bigl(n\times[B]-\mu_0K\bigr)\psi\,dS\,dt$$
against every scalar $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$ (the vector integrals being componentwise) are well defined by the ordinary
surface-and-time integrals, with no product of distributions formed; these
vanishing pairings are the precise weak form of the four jump identities, and
they do vanish. The identities then hold for $dS\,dt$-almost every $(x,t)$;
since the traces are spatially continuous at each fixed time, they hold for
every $x\in S$ for almost every $t\in I$. They hold at every $(x,t)$ whenever
the jump densities are additionally jointly continuous. Merely having
one-sided spatial $C^1$ traces separately at every time does not justify this
last upgrade.

Throughout, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the surface integral of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and the domains of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] are developed under that convention.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open. Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface ([[def-codimension-and-hypersurface]], [[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]): every $p\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^2\times\{0\})$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Such an $S$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, so the surface integral and the surface measure $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf 1_A\,dS$ of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]] apply; that measure is finite. The slice-chart definition has no manifold boundary; $S$ has no edge. If $S$ is empty, all surface functionals below are zero and the estimates are read separately without taking a supremum over the empty set.

A **two-sided presentation** of $S$ consists of a continuous unit normal field $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ together with sides: $n(x)$ is orthogonal to $S$ at $x$ in the sense that $\langle n(x),\gamma'(0)\rangle=0$ for every $C^1$ path $\gamma:(-1,1)\to S$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\lVert n(x)\rVert_2=1$; and $\Omega_-,\Omega_+\subseteq\Omega$ are open sets with

$$\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+,\qquad \Omega_-\cap\Omega_+=\varnothing,$$

such that for every $x\in S$ there is $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(x)>0$ with $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_+$ for all $0<s<\varepsilon$ and $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_-$ for all $-\varepsilon<s<0$. The normal $n$ points from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$; the orientation convention for normals is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

**The surface distribution $\delta_S$.** For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS,$$

where the right-hand side is the surface integral of the restriction of $\psi$ to $S$, taken in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; complex-valued $\psi$ are integrated componentwise in real and imaginary parts. For a continuous **density** $a:S\to\mathbb R$ define

$$a\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S a\,\psi\,dS .$$

Both are complex-linear functionals on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, and both are distributions: $\delta_S,a\delta_S\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[def-distribution]]).

**Jumps across $S$.** Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be a field that is of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately and has one-sided continuous traces: there are continuous maps $F_+,F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3$ with

$$F_+(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_+}}F(y),\qquad F_-(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_-}}F(y)$$

for every $x\in S$, the limits taken in $\mathbb R^3$. The **jump of $F$ across $S$** is the continuous map

$$[F]:=F_+-F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3 .$$

No continuity of $F$ across $S$ is assumed or implied; $F$ need not even be defined on $S$, and the two traces may differ.

### Well-definedness and finite order

*The surface functionals are distributions.* Fix a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ with the seminorm $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K|\psi|$ of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. Since $\psi$ vanishes outside $K$ and is continuous, $\sup_S|\psi|\le p_0(\psi)$; and $\int_S|a\psi|\,dS\le\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\sup_S|\psi|\,S(S)$ with $\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}<\infty$ by compactness of $S$ and continuity of $a$. Hence

$$|\delta_S(\psi)|\le S(S)\,p_0(\psi),\qquad |a\delta_S(\psi)|\le \lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\,S(S)\,p_0(\psi),$$

a finite-order estimate of order $0$ with constants independent of $K$; by the local finite-order characterization ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]) both functionals are distributions. This is the sense in which boundedness on the compact interface and finiteness of the surface measure give continuity of finite order. Linearity is immediate from linearity of the integral; the pairing is complex bilinear with no conjugation, as in [[def-distribution]].

*The field has locally integrable components.* The hypersurface $S$ is a Lebesgue-null set of $\mathbb R^3$: by the slice-chart property it is covered by finitely many compact pieces each of which is, in suitable $C^2$ coordinates, a graph over a compact subset of a coordinate plane, hence has content zero ([[thm-graph-of-continuous-function-on-a-compact-set-has-content-zero]]), and each piece has content zero in the ambient coordinates because it is the image under the $C^1$ chart inverse of a compact content-zero set ([[lem-c-one-images-of-content-zero-compact-sets-have-content-zero]]); a finite union of compact content-zero sets is compact and null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]), hence has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $S$ has content zero in the sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. Now $F$ is continuous on $\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$. For each $x\in S$, the two one-sided limits are finite; hence there is a neighbourhood $U_x$ of $x$ on which $|F|$ is bounded on each side (use the defining limit with tolerance $1$ for each of $F_+(x)$ and $F_-(x)$). Away from $S$, continuity also gives a neighbourhood with a finite bound at every point. For a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, these neighbourhoods cover $K$; take a finite subcover and the maximum of its finitely many bounds. This gives a finite $M_K$ such that $|F|\le M_K$ on $K\setminus S$. Extend $F$ by zero on the null closed set $S$; the extension is measurable because the two side restrictions are continuous, and

$$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le M_K\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

the contributions from $K\cap S$ being null. Thus the components of $F$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], and define a regular distribution; the trace condition is exactly what makes the boundary values $F_\pm$ well-defined continuous functions on $S$, so the jump $[F]$ is continuous and bounded on $S$.

### Conventions and exclusions

The sign convention is fixed by the normal: $n$ points from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, so $[F]=F_+-F_-$ is measured in the direction of $n$. This convention is used by the interface-derivative lemma on this page, where $\operatorname{div}F$ and $\operatorname{curl}F$ acquire the surface terms $n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S$ and $n\times[F]\,\delta_S$; reversing $n$ reverses the signs of both sides consistently. The definition assumes a fixed stationary interface $S$: no time dependence of $S$ is part of the data, and the stationary jump formulas are not asserted for moving interfaces. The density $a$ is continuous, so $a\delta_S$ is defined by the displayed integral; no product of two arbitrary distributions, and no product of $\delta_S$ with a merely locally integrable field, is defined here. The definition is stated under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ because the surface measure it invokes is; the positivity of the surface measure of nonempty open pieces of $S$, and the finite-order estimates above, are its only uses here.

Under the Countable Choice convention of the stated boundary and sheet-distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), adopt as a physical model of ideal electrostatic conductors, for the classical laboratory framework of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]: a **conductor configuration** consists of the following data, and every model of this postulate is required to satisfy the clauses below. No experiment is reported and no empirical value is inferred; this is an explicitly adopted equilibrium idealization together with its geometric and source conventions.

(a) [Geometry] a laboratory region $\Omega\times I$ with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ an arbitrary open ambient region, a finite family $D_1,\dots,D_m$ ($m\ge1$) of bounded $C^\infty$ domains with pairwise disjoint closures in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] with closures strictly inside $\Omega$ (the **conductor bodies**), the **conductor** $D:=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_m$, its **surface** $\partial D$, and the **vacuum region** $\Omega_v:=\Omega\setminus\overline D$. By [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]], $\partial D=\partial D_1\cup\cdots\cup\partial D_m$ is a disjoint union of compact embedded $C^\infty$ hypersurfaces. The vacuum $\Omega_v$ is open, and near each conductor surface it is locally the smooth exterior side of that conductor. No boundedness or regularity of the ambient boundary is inferred from openness. In the additional **bounded smooth ambient branch**, assume that $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^\infty$ domain; only then [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]] gives that $\Omega_v$ is a bounded $C^\infty$ domain with the specified outer/conductor boundary charts; we additionally require $\Omega_v$ to be connected (configurations whose vacuum region is separated by the conductors, for instance by an enclosing closed shell, are outside this model as formulated here).

(b) [Equilibrium and sources] the configuration is in the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] on the vacuum region: $B=0$, $J=0$, $E$ is the fixed-time electric field of [[def-em-fields]], the volume source density $\rho_v$ is a continuous real map on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ (C m$^{-3}$, [[def-em-sources]]) extended by zero to $D$; the **conductor charge is a stationary surface charge**, i.e. a continuous density $\sigma:\partial D\to\mathbb R$ (C m$^{-2}$) whose pairing with test functions is the stationary-sheet source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) with tangential current $K=0$ and $S=\partial D$; and the field pair $(E,0)$ together with the source pair $(\rho_v+\sigma\,\delta_{\partial D},\ 0)$ satisfies the adopted distributional vacuum Maxwell equations [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]]. Inside the conductor the field vanishes: $E\equiv0$ on $D$ (the **equilibrium condition**); equivalently the conductor interior is field-free and carries no volume charge.

(c) [Potential and equipotential convention] there is a function $\varphi\in C^0(\Omega)\cap C^2(\Omega_v)$ with $E=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\Omega_v$ and with $\varphi$ constant on each conductor body, $\varphi|_{D_j}\equiv V_j$ for real constants $V_j$ (volts, [[def-em-si-conventions]]); by continuity of $\varphi$ the trace of $\varphi$ on each $\partial D_j$ from the vacuum side equals $V_j$ as well. This is the single-function convention of an ideal conductor with no double layer: the model reads the same potential value on both sides of $\partial D_j$, while the normal component of $E$ may jump.

(d) [Data] a model is completed either by the component potentials $V_1,\dots,V_m$ together with the volume source $\rho_v$ and the data on $\partial\Omega$ where the laboratory region is bounded, or by the component total charges $Q_j:=\int_{\partial D_j}\sigma\,dS$ (C) together with those same ambient data. These are two declared data types; the postulate asserts neither that both data types are simultaneously specifiable nor that either is solvable for arbitrary data.

(e) [Scope] This is a static, frame-relative equilibrium idealization: it excludes transient finite-conductivity dynamics, relaxation to equilibrium, moving surface charge, electrode polarization and contact effects, and it is not derived from a microscopic matter model. It asserts no existence or uniqueness theorem (those are separate conditional results), no force, no energy, no radiation, no measurement and no apparatus realization; the value $V_j$ is a model parameter and the surface density $\sigma$ is an idealization variable determined by the equilibrium problem when it is solvable. The general open ambient branch retains compact conductor bodies in exterior configurations. Its additional bounded smooth ambient branch is distinct from the separately declared grounded-half-space and infinite parallel-plane idealizations, whose conductor bodies are themselves noncompact. Those examples retain the equilibrium/equipotential interpretation but their noncompact bodies and plane distributions are not instances of this compact-body configuration or its compact-sheet predicate. No arbitrary exterior solvability is asserted.

For a bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega$ and $u\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, the classical normal derivative is $\partial_
u u(x)=Du(x)\cdot
u(x)$ on $\partial\Omega$. Here Du is the continuous extension of the interior gradient and $
u$ is the outward unit normal. For a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation define the same expression on each face off its edge set E; arbitrary values on E do not change a surface integral. This definition uses a classical continuous trace, and asserts neither a Sobolev trace nor a conormal derivative.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the boundary-chart and surface-measure interfaces cited below ([[def-countable-choice]]); no other choice principle is used. Let $k\ge1$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^k$ domain in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] (nonempty, bounded, open, and locally exactly the one-sided subgraph of a $C^k$ graph function over a hyperplane). Then:

(a) [Compactness and finiteness] $\partial D$ is nonempty and compact; the complement $\mathbb R^3\setminus\partial D$ need not be connected here. Moreover $\partial D$ has finitely many connected components, and each connected component of $\partial D$ is compact.

(b) [Finite embedded presentation] the local boundary charts give finitely many regular injective $C^k$ parametrisations of $\partial D$ with $C^k$ coordinate transitions, of the graph type required by [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]: writing a chart as $R(p)=(y,s)$, the graph map $y\mapsto R^{-1}(y,h(y))$ is injective, of class $C^k$, with $C^k$ inverse (the inverse is $p\mapsto\pi(R(p))$ restricted to the graph, where $\pi(y,s)=y$); consequently $\partial D$ is a compact embedded $C^k$ hypersurface, and for $k\ge1$ it carries the finite surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]].

(c) [Normal field] the outward unit normal $\nu$ of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a continuous unit normal field on $\partial D$, with $\nu(x)$ orthogonal to the tangent plane of the graph chart at each $x$; it is the field used by the Green and divergence items cited by this page's consumers.

The statement is geometric: it asserts no differentiability of $D$ beyond $C^k$, no boundedness of chart derivatives beyond the compact patches, and no connectedness of either $D$ or $\partial D$.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

This gives $n\cdot E_+=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ and $\sigma=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot E_+$, and $n\times E_+=0$, which is (a); if $\sigma=0$ at a point then $n\cdot E_+=0$ and $n\times E_+=0$ there, so $E_+=0$ by [F6], and the sign of $\sigma$ is the sign of $n\cdot E_+$ since $\varepsilon_0>0$.

Equipotential boundary traces. For $x\in\partial D_j$, the boundary definition supplies points of $D_j$ arbitrarily close to $x$. Since $\varphi$ is continuous on $\Omega$ and $\varphi|_{D_j}=V_j$ [F1], its value and vacuum trace at $x$ equal $V_j$. Thus the trace is constant on all of $\partial D_j$, and in particular on every connected component contained there. The separated boundary pieces partition $S$ [F5], so this proves (c) directly from the model's continuous equipotential convention.

On the vacuum side $E=-
abla\varphi$ [F1], so $
abla\varphi_+=-E_+$ [F4] and $\partial\varphi/\partial n=

u=-n$ [F3], so $\partial\varphi/\partial
u=
abla\varphi_+\cdot
u=-
abla\varphi_+\cdot n=-\partial\varphi/\partial n=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ by [step 2.1]; integrating over $\partial D_j$ gives $Q_j=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}\partial\varphi/\partial
u\,dS$. This is (d).

Data reading and scope. boundaries.evidence: The vacuum region is a bounded C^infinity domain with finitely many components (possibly one) and nonempty boundary ([F3]); the homogeneous difference data of step 2.2 is the zero-data case.
Zero source and zero boundary data are included: steps 1.1/1.2/2.1 apply verbatim to rho=0 or to vanishing differences, and step 3.1 uses the zero potential as one of the two exterior witnesses.
One connected component with one additive constant per component is exactly the finite-component statement of step 1.2; the single-component case of the weak branches is step 1.3.

The degenerate case of a vanishing difference on the boundary (homogeneous Dirichlet data) is step 2.2 via Green's identity; the geometry is nondegenerate because the domain is bounded and C^infinity by hypothesis.
Step 3.1 evaluates the limits of the exterior witness at |x|=R and as |x| tends to infinity; the classical statements are formulated on closures C^2(Omega-bar).

Full AC is declared for the weak-solvability and trace suppliers used in (c) and enters through [F4]-[F6] in step 1.3; the classical clauses (a),(b) and the witness of (e) add no choice beyond the declared conventions.
The forward implications of (b) are step 1.2 (equal Neumann data imply a constant difference via [F2]) and step 2.1 (any classical solution satisfies the flux identity).
The reverse direction of (b) is also step 1.2: adding one constant per component preserves both the Poisson equation and the Neumann data; the combined reading of both directions is stated there.
