citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) inherited from the Newtonian, polar and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let

$$H:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_3>0\},\qquad \Pi:=\{x_3=0\},\qquad p:=a e_3\ (a>0),$$

Here $e_3:=(0,0,1)$ is the third coordinate unit vector, $a$ carries metres, and the coordinates are SI numerical readings in the named frame. Let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a charge parameter (coulombs) and $\varepsilon_0>0$ the framework constant ([[def-em-si-conventions]]). Define, with arbitrary values on the exceptional sets,

$$\varphi_I(x):=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac1{|x-p|}-\frac1{|x+ae_3|}\right)\quad(x\in H\setminus\{p\}),\qquad E_I:=-\nabla\varphi_I.$$

The map $E_I$ is a spatial field of [[def-em-fields]] in the fixed-time reading, with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Then:

(a) [Candidate field] $\varphi_I\in C^\infty(H\setminus\{p\})$ and $\Delta\varphi_I=0$ pointwise on $H\setminus\{p\}$: the first term is the Coulomb potential of $p$, whose $n=3$ fundamental solution is harmonic off its pole ([[lem-laplace-fundamental-solution-is-harmonic-off-its-pole]], [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]](d)), and the second term is $C^\infty$ and harmonic on the whole of $H$ because its pole $-ae_3$ lies outside $H$; $E_I$ is $C^\infty$ on $H\setminus\{p\}$.

(b) [Distributional point source] $\varphi_I\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(H)$ and

$$-\Delta T_{\varphi_I}=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\,\delta_p\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(H),$$

where $T_{\varphi_I}$ is the regular distribution of $\varphi_I$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\delta_p$ the Dirac distribution at $p$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); moreover the field satisfies $\operatorname{div}E_I=(q/\varepsilon_0)\delta_p$ and $\operatorname{curl}E_I=0$ in $\mathcal D'(H)$, where the divergence and curl of $E_I$ are the distributional derivatives of its components ([[def-distributional-derivative]]). Thus $(E_I,0)$ is a pure electrostatic model on $H$ with the fixed-time point source $q\delta_p$, the static reading of the stationary point charge of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e)).

(c) [Boundary trace and decay] $\varphi_I$ extends continuously to $\overline H\setminus\{p\}$ with $\varphi_I=0$ on $\Pi$ (the two denominators are equal there), and for $|x|\ge2a$ the cancellation bound holds:

$$|\varphi_I(x)|\le\frac{2|q|\,a}{\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2}.$$

The bound follows by applying the mean value theorem along the segment from $-ae_3$ to $ae_3$ to the function $y\mapsto|x-y|^{-1}$, whose gradient is bounded by $(|x|-a)^{-2}$ there ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). In particular $\varphi_I(x)\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in $H$.

(d) [Uniqueness in the declared class] let $\psi:H\setminus\{p\}\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and harmonic on $H\setminus\{p\}$, continuous on $\overline H\setminus\{p\}$, with $\psi=0$ on $\Pi$, $|x-p|(\psi(x)-\varphi_I(x))\to0$ as $x\to p$ and $\psi(x)\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in $H$. Then $\psi=\varphi_I$ on $H\setminus\{p\}$. Equivalently, the Dirichlet problem $\Delta\psi=0$ on $H\setminus\{p\}$, $\psi=0$ on $\Pi$, with the leading singularity of the point charge at $p$ and decay at infinity, has exactly one solution in the stated class.

(e) [Physics reading: ideal grounded plane in the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]] the ideal grounded conducting half-space $\{x_3<0\}$ with the field $E_I$ on $H$, $E\equiv0$ below $\Pi$ and the induced density $\sigma:=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot E_+|_\Pi=-\varepsilon_0\,\partial_3\varphi_I|_\Pi$ (using the normal $n=e_3$ from the conductor into the vacuum; $\sigma\in C^\infty(\Pi)$) is a model of the same equilibrium structure as [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]]: it is a pure electrostatic field on $H$ with the point source at $p$ and the equipotential boundary condition $\varphi_I=0$ on $\Pi$; the pair $(E_I,0)$ satisfies the static electrostatic equations with source $q\delta_p$ on $H$, and the induced density is explicitly $\sigma(x_1,x_2)=-qa/[2\pi(x_1^2+x_2^2+a^2)^{3/2}]$, is absolutely integrable over the plane, and has total charge $\int_\Pi\sigma\,dS=-q$. However, the half-space conductor is not a compact conductor body: the plane is not a compact embedded hypersurface, $\Pi$ and $\{x_3<0\}$ are not among the geometric objects of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]], the density $\sigma$ is not a declared stationary-sheet source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c), and the noncompact plane pairing is not an adopted compact-sheet source of that definition. As a separately specified mathematical idealization, extending $E_I$ by zero below the plane gives $\operatorname{div}\widetilde E=(q\delta_p+\sigma\delta_\Pi)/\varepsilon_0$ and $\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$, where $(\sigma\delta_\Pi)(\eta)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\sigma(x')\eta(x',0)dx'$. This verified identity does not extend the framework postulate to arbitrary noncompact sheets. The clause is the explicitly declared idealization whose exact mathematical content is (a)-(d).

(f) [Scope] the statement concerns the ideal point charge above an ideal grounded plane in the declared decay class; it excludes finite-plane edge effects, conductor thickness, transients, moving charges, radiation, self-force and any measurement; no uniqueness is asserted outside the class of (d), and the point-source singularity is never evaluated.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]).
Work in $\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]) and the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$.
Use one-based labels $v_i:=v(i-1)$ for vectors $v\in\mathbb R^3$, $i=1,2,3$; $\partial_i$ means the derivative in that coordinate (the supplier's $\partial_{i-1}$), and $e_i$ below is the standard unit vector in that direction. Divergence, curl and gradient are the cited operators with these labels, so relabelling does not change them.
Let $\Phi$ be the $n=3$ fundamental solution of $-\Delta$ of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], normalised by $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$; then $\omega_2=4\pi$ and
$$\Phi(z)=\frac{1}{4\pi|z|}\qquad(z\ne0)$$
([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).
Let $Nf$ be the Newtonian potential of [[def-newtonian-potential]].

(a) [Smooth compact sources] Let $\rho:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ with compact support contained in $\overline B_R$, $R>0$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-metric-ball]]), put $\varphi:=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$ and $E:=-\nabla\varphi$.
Then $\varphi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ ([[thm-newtonian-potential-for-holder-data-is-classical]]), and pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$
$$-\Delta\varphi=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0$$
with the operators of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]].
Moreover, with $Q:=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ the absolutely convergent Coulomb integral representation holds, and its far-field bound holds for $|x|>2R$,
$$E(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{x-y}{|x-y|^3}\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad |E(x)|\le\frac{\| \rho\|_1}{\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2}\quad(|x|>2R),$$
and for $|x|>2R$ the potential obeys the decay bound $|\varphi(x)|\le |Q|/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|)+R\|\rho\|_1/(\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2)$ ([[lem-em-newtonian-far-field-gradient]], [[thm-decay-of-the-newtonian-potential-of-compactly-supported-data]]).
The pair $(E,0,\rho,0)$ therefore realises the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with source $\rho$, and $E$ is the field of the localised Newtonian potential.

(b) [Uniqueness with vanishing at infinity] If $\psi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfies $-\Delta\psi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$ and $\lim_{|x|\to\infty}\psi(x)=0$, then $\psi=\varphi$ ([[thm-weak-maximum-principle-for-the-laplacian]]).
In particular, among $C^2$ solutions of the Poisson equation of a compactly supported $C^1$ source decaying at infinity, the localised Newtonian potential is the unique one.

(c) [Compactly supported $L^1$ sources] If instead $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is real, measurable and compactly supported, then $N\rho$ is finite $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere, belongs to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, is $C^\infty$ and harmonic off the support of $\rho$, and its regular distribution satisfies
$$-\Delta T_{\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho}=T_{\rho/\varepsilon_0}\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$$
([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]], scaled by $\varepsilon_0^{-1}$; [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(d) [Point charge] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and define, with arbitrary values at $x_0$,
$$\varphi_q(x):=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|},\qquad E_q(x):=\frac{q\,(x-x_0)}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|^3}\qquad(x\ne x_0).$$
Then $\varphi_q\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $E_q$ is locally integrable and $C^\infty$ off $x_0$, $E_q=-\nabla\varphi_q$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{x_0\}$, and, with $T_{\varphi_q}$ the regular distribution of $\varphi_q$ and $\operatorname{div}E_q:=\sum_i\partial_iT_{E_{q,i}}$, $\operatorname{curl}E_q:=(\partial_2T_{E_{q,3}}-\partial_3T_{E_{q,2}},\ \partial_3T_{E_{q,1}}-\partial_1T_{E_{q,3}},\ \partial_1T_{E_{q,2}}-\partial_2T_{E_{q,1}})$,
$$-\Delta T_{\varphi_q}=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\delta_{x_0},\qquad \operatorname{div}E_q=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\delta_{x_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E_q=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$$
([[thm-minus-laplacian-of-the-fundamental-solution-is-dirac]] for the first identity, [[lem-em-distributional-gradient-smooth-off-a-point]] for the passage from the potential to the field, [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).
The distribution $q\delta_{x_0}$ is the fixed-time reading of the stationary point charge of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with charge parameter $q$ and constant trajectory $z\equiv x_0$ ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e)); so the pair $(E_q,0)$ satisfies the distributional pure electrostatic equations with that point source.
This is an idealised point-source model: no claim of uniqueness for the point source, no self-force and no statement about the field at $x_0$ itself is made.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

**Clause 1 is about an arbitrary norm; clauses 2 to 4 are about
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $n \ge 1$.**

1. **Finite and reverse triangle inequalities.** Let $V$ be a vector space over
   $\mathbb{R}$ and $N$ a norm on it ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$ and every list $u : p \to V$
   ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]),
   $$N\Bigl(\sum_{j<p} u_j\Bigr) \;\le\; \sum_{j<p} N(u_j),$$
   and for all $u, w \in V$,
   $$\bigl|N(u) - N(w)\bigr| \;\le\; N(u - w).$$

Now let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ carry the norms of
[[def-p-norms-on-rn]] and write $\iota$ for the canonical natural
([[def-canonical-natural]]).

2. **Every norm is dominated by the $1$-norm.** Let $N$ be a norm on
   $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and put $C := \max\{\, N(e_k) : k<n \,\}$, a maximum over a
   nonempty finite set of reals ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]],
   [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). Then $C \ge 0$ and
   $$N(x) \;\le\; C\,\lVert x\rVert_1 \qquad \text{for every } x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}.$$
3. **The comparison chain.** For every $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2 \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_1 \;\le\; \iota(n)\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty , \qquad \lVert x\rVert_1 \;\le\; \sqrt{\iota(n)}\;\lVert x\rVert_2 .$$
   In particular $\lVert\cdot\rVert_1$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and
   $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ are pairwise equivalent norms on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   with the constants displayed ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).
4. **Every norm is Lipschitz for the Euclidean metric.** With $N$ and $C$ as in
   clause 2, $N : (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2) \to (\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is
   Lipschitz with constant $C\sqrt{\iota(n)}$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]],
   [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), hence uniformly continuous and
   continuous ([[thm-metric-regularity-hierarchy]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

**Where $n \ge 1$ enters.** Clauses 2 and 4 need the maximum defining $C$ to
exist, and clause 3 mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$; at $n = 0$ each is a
maximum over the empty index set and does not exist, exactly as in
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] and [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]. Clause 1 carries no hypothesis
on the dimension and no hypothesis on the space.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Adopt as physical postulates of this framework, on the spacetime and particle
model of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and
[[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] and on the special-relativity particle
model [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]:

(i) [Test charge in a prescribed external field] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a
constant charge parameter ([[def-em-sources]]), $m>0$ an externally supplied
rest mass, $x:J\to A$ a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline with
four-velocity $U$, and let $F$ be a prescribed field of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph
of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle. Adopt the equation of
motion

$$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),$$

where, at each original parameter $s\in J$, $\Phi=\Phi_{x(s)}$ is the
raised-index operator of the field at $x(s)$, defined by
$\eta(\Phi_{x(s)}(u),w)=F(x(s))(w,u)$
([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]); equivalently
$m\,dU^\mu/d\tau=q\,F^{\mu\nu}U_\nu$. Here $dU/d\tau$ is the derivative of $U$
with respect to its proper-time function $\tau(s)$: explicitly
$dU/d\tau=U'(s)/\tau'(s)$, with
$\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}>0$. It is the four-acceleration of the worldline
([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). The particle's own field
is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no
self-force.

(ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of
[[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated
matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density
$\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit
W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the
spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local
interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed
current alone.

(iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within
electromagnetism. The coupling is adopted for constant $q$ and $m>0$; no
magnetic-monopole coupling, no radiation reaction and no self-force are
included. In particular the nonrelativistic coordinate statement
$mr''=q(E+r'\times B)$ is not adopted as exact: the adopted statement is the
covariant one of clause (i), and any low-speed statement requires its own
approximation hypotheses and error bounds.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Let the laboratory region, its inertial chart and the fields and sources be those
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], with the
units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; fix the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the chart and the oriented volume form $\varepsilon$ of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]], with $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$ and
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$.

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

(b) [Observer decomposition] Let $n:=e_0$ be the future unit timelike vector of
the chart and let $e_a:=F_{ab}n^b$, $b_a:=(*F)_{ab}n^b$ be the observer
components of [[thm-sr-antisymmetric-observer-decomposition]]; then
$e_i=+E_i/c$, $b_i=-B_i$ and $e_0=b_0=0$, and the invariants and square wedge
of that theorem read

$$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=+4\,(E\cdot B)/c,\qquad F\wedge F=-2\,(E\cdot B)\,\varepsilon/c,$$

where $|\cdot|$ and $\cdot$ are the spatial Euclidean structure of the frame.
(For the same pair $(E,B)$, that theorem's optional clause (d) uses
$F_{\rm optional}^{i0}=E_i/c$ and $F_{\rm optional}^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, so
$F_{\rm optional}=-F$ in all six components, not only the magnetic block. This
framework fixes clause (a) and uses the theorem's general algebra; its optional
SI dictionary must be converted by negating the entire tensor.)

(c) [Potentials when they exist] If $\varphi$ and $A$ are $C^1$ with
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$A^\mu:=(\varphi/c,A)$, $A_\mu:=\eta_{\mu\nu}A^\nu$, then
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$; conversely, if a $C^1$
covector field $A_\mu$ on $U$ satisfies $F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu
-\partial_\nu A_\mu$, then $E,B$ recovered from $F$ by clause (a) obey
$E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with
$\varphi:=-cA_0$ and the spatial potential vector $A:=(A_1,A_2,A_3)$. Here
$\nabla$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] in the spatial coordinates,
and the spatial cross-product conventions of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] are
used. The definition does not assert that every field pair admits such a
potential; where a $C^1$ potential represents the $C^1$-or-better field of
clause (a), the field is closed in the explicit sense
$\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}=0$. This conclusion does not require second
classical derivatives of the potential: put
$H_{\lambda\mu\nu}:=\partial_\lambda F_{\mu\nu}+\partial_\mu F_{\nu\lambda}
+\partial_\nu F_{\lambda\mu}$, which is continuous because $F$ is $C^1$; for
every smooth compactly supported test $\psi$, substituting $F=dA$ and
integrating by parts twice, moving the derivatives first onto $\psi$
([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]] (b)) and then off the
potential factors after commuting only the smooth test derivatives
([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]), gives $\int H\psi=0$; the
fundamental lemma (a) of [[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]
then gives $H=0$. The framework's potential theorems establish existence only
under their stated hypotheses; [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]
supplies the coordinate derivatives $\partial_\mu$ used throughout.

(d) [Four-current and index-raising operator] With the adopted four-current
$j=(c\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]], the raised-index operator $\Phi$ of
[[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]], defined pointwise on $V$ by
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$, satisfies
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$; the components of $F$
carry the tesla (T), those of $j$ carry A m$^{-2}$, and those of a
four-potential $A^\mu$ carry T m.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

derivations.claim:
External field. By [F1], $E_{m ext}=E_I-E_q=-
abla(\varphi_I-\varphi_q^p)=-
abla u$ on the punctured half-space, and $u$ is $C^\infty$ on the ball $|x-p|<a$ [F1, F4]. By [F2] with $c=+ae_3$, $
abla u(x)=+\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{x+ae_3}{|x+ae_3|^3}$ there, so at $x=p=ae_3$ one has $
abla u(p)=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2ae_3}{(2a)^3}=\dfrac{q\,e_3}{16\pi\varepsilon_0a^2}$ and $E_{m ext}(p)=-
abla u(p)=-\dfrac{q}{16\pi\varepsilon_0a^2}e_3$. This is (a).
Force. By [F3] applied at the instantaneous rest state of the held charge, the force is $F=qE_{\rm ext}(p)$; substituting [step 1.1] gives $F=-\dfrac{q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0a^2}e_3$. This is (b).

Signs, magnitude and scope. Since $q^2\ge0$ with equality exactly for $q=0$, the vector $F$ is a nonpositive multiple of $e_3$: for $q\ne0$ it points from $p$ toward the plane and has magnitude $q^2/(16\pi\varepsilon_0a^2)$, while $q=0$ gives $F=0$. The self-field $E_q$ is excluded from the coupling by [F3], so the computation is the external mirror force and not a self-force; the induced total plane charge $-q$ and the concentration of the induced distribution under the charge are the ideal-plane statements of [[pthm-em-image-method-certificate]](e), and the held trajectory is not claimed to solve any dynamics. This is (c).

boundaries.evidence: The unit ball B is nonempty and its boundary S^2 is nonempty (step 1.1); the impossible object is the solution set, shown empty in steps 2.1 and 4.1, not any domain of the statement.
The volume source is zero throughout; the companion zero-boundary-field case is step 2.3; the zero datum would satisfy the compatibility and is not the subject.
The single constant datum g=1 and the single test v=1 drive the obstruction (steps 2.2/4.1); a single ball is treated.
The degenerate vanishing-area case is impossible: step 1.1 computes |S^2|=4pi>0, and S^2 is a compact embedded smooth hypersurface so no corner or edge degeneracy occurs.

Full AC for the trace and Sobolev interfaces and AC_omega for surface measure are declared; step 2.2 uses the boundedness of the H^{1/2} to L^2 inclusion and the trace theorem, and step 4.1 the solvability criterion.

The direction used is the necessity half of the solvability criterion [F4]: existence of a weak solution implies the value of the data functional at the constant is zero; its contrapositive with l(1)=4pi excludes solutions in step 4.1.

citations.quote: Assume $\Omega$ is bounded with $C^1$ boundary, $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$, $f=-\Delta u$, and outward normal derivative $g=\partial_\nu u$. Then $\int_\Omega f=-\int_{\partial\Omega}g$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

For a bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega$ and $u\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, the classical normal derivative is $\partial_
u u(x)=Du(x)\cdot
u(x)$ on $\partial\Omega$. Here Du is the continuous extension of the interior gradient and $
u$ is the outward unit normal. For a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation define the same expression on each face off its edge set E; arbitrary values on E do not change a surface integral. This definition uses a classical continuous trace, and asserts neither a Sobolev trace nor a conormal derivative.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), the convention of the boundary-chart and surface-measure interfaces used below ([[def-countable-choice]]).
Use the explicit coordinate labels $x_k:=x(k-1)$ for $k=1,2,3$; these relabel the zero-based coordinates of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
On $\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]) let $0<\varepsilon<R$ and put
$$B_R:=\{x:|x|<R\},\qquad \overline B_R:=\{x:|x|\le R\},\qquad A_{\varepsilon,R}:=\{x:\varepsilon<|x|<R\},\qquad S_r:=\{x:|x|=r\}.$$
Then:

(a) [Domains] $B_R$ and $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ are bounded $C^1$ domains in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; their boundaries are $S_R$, respectively $S_\varepsilon\cup S_R$, and the corresponding outward unit normals are
$$\nu(x)=\frac{x}{|x|}\ \ (x\in S_R),\qquad \nu(x)=-\frac{x}{|x|}\ \ (x\in S_\varepsilon,\ \text{boundary of }A_{\varepsilon,R});$$

(b) [Spheres] each $S_r$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ (indeed $C^\infty$) hypersurface in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] with two-sided unit normals $\pm x/|x|$, and the boundary components $S_\varepsilon,S_R$, each subdivided into six compact signed-maximal-coordinate graph faces $F_{r,k,\sigma}:=\{x\in S_r:\sigma x_k\ge |x_j|\text{ for all }j\}$ ($k=1,2,3$, $\sigma=\pm1$), with the compact edge set consisting of their seams $\sigma x_k=|x_j|$ for $j\ne k$, give a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ in the sense of [[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]];

(c) [Consequences used downstream] the divergence theorem and Green's first identity of [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]] and [[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] apply on $B_R$ and on $A_{\varepsilon,R}$ with the outward normals of (a), and $S_r$ carries a finite Borel surface measure with the standard graph charts.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.
For every $n\ge1$, $V_n(1)=\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2+1)$. Here $n$ is an integer.
For every $s>0$, $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$, and $\Gamma(1)=1$.
$\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the boundary
conventions of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a bounded $C^1$ domain, let
$0<s<1$, $1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix a
finite family of boundary charts: for each $j$ let $W_j\subseteq\mathbb R^n$
be open and $\Phi_j:W_j\to\Phi_j(W_j)\subseteq B_j\times\mathbb R$ a
flattening chart as in
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], so that
$\Phi_j(\Omega\cap W_j)=\Phi_j(W_j)\cap\{t<0\}$ and the boundary corresponds
to the graph $\{t=0\}$; write $\Psi_j:=\pi\circ\Phi_j|_{\partial\Omega\cap W_j}$
for the induced parametrisation of $\partial\Omega\cap W_j$ by an open subset
$V_j:=\Psi_j(\partial\Omega\cap W_j)\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and assume the
$\partial\Omega\cap W_j$ cover $\partial\Omega$. Fix a subordinate finite
ambient partition: nonnegative $\chi_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with
$\operatorname{supp}\chi_j\subseteq W_j$ and $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ on a
neighbourhood of $\partial\Omega$
([[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]]).
Finally let $\partial\Omega$ carry the chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], which fixes the
meaning of almost-everywhere equality and of $L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).

For a Borel function $g:\partial\Omega\to\mathbb K$ put
$$\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)}:=\sum_j\bigl\|(\chi_jg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}\bigr\|_{W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{n-1})},$$
where the chart representation $(\chi_jg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}$ is read in graph
coordinates and extended by zero off $V_j$, and the norm on the right is that
of [[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]. The **fractional
Sobolev space of the boundary** is
$$W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K):=\{g\in L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K):\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega)}<\infty\}.$$
The right-hand side is a finite sum of finite norms of compactly supported
chart representations, so $W^{s,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is exactly the
set of $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ classes whose chart representations all lie in
the Euclidean space of
[[def-fractional-slobodeckij-space-on-euclidean-space]]; that the resulting
space and the topology of the norm do not depend on the choices of atlas and
partition, up to equivalence of norms, is proved in
[[lem-fractional-boundary-norm-is-independent-of-atlas]] and is not assumed
here.

Three conventions belong to the definition. First, membership is a property of
the $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ class: $g$ is an almost-everywhere class with respect
to the surface measure, and the chart representations are classes in
$W^{s,p}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$; representative independence for the Euclidean
factor is established together with the well-definedness lemma on this page
and is not presupposed here. Second, the norm is a finite sum
over a finite atlas, and each $\chi_jg$ is supported in the interior of the
chart, so the localisations are compactly supported and no boundary behaviour
of $\Psi_j^{-1}$ outside $V_j$ enters. Third, on this page the exponent used
is the trace exponent $s=\theta=1-1/p$ for $1<p<\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the actually cited Sobolev trace, lift and mean-zero density interfaces, and its Countable Choice consequence for the measure and variational interfaces ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain, let $\varepsilon$ be measurable symmetric uniformly elliptic ([[lem-em-prescribed-fractional-dirichlet-existence]]), let $\rho\in L^2(\Omega)$, and let $g\in H^{-1/2}(\partial\Omega)$, the bounded real dual of the boundary trace space ([[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]). Define $\ell(v)=\int_\Omega\rho v+\langle g,Tv\rangle$ on $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]). A weak Neumann solution is a $u\in H^1$ with

$$\int_\Omega\nabla v\cdot\varepsilon\nabla u=\ell(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1(\Omega).$$

Such a solution exists if and only if $\ell(1)=0$, and is then unique up to an additive constant; normalising $\int_\Omega u=0$ makes it unique. On finitely many connected components the compatibility and normalisation are imposed separately on each component. For finitely many disjoint smooth stationary interfaces with piecewise smooth uniformly elliptic $\varepsilon$, bulk data $\rho\in L^2$ and prescribed sheet charge $\sigma$ on the interfaces defining a bounded trace functional on $H^1$ (for instance $\sigma\in L^2$ of each smooth compact interface), the same argument gives weak Dirichlet or compatible Neumann existence for the transmission problem, with the globally $H^1$ potential having identical one-sided trace; where the solution is classically smooth on each side, integration by parts gives the jump $n\cdot[\varepsilon\nabla u]=-\sigma$, equivalently $n\cdot[D]=\sigma$ for the explicitly defined mathematical flux $D:=-\varepsilon\nabla u$ on each side. General piecewise classical regularity remains a separate requirement.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$
