$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the cited weak-solvability and trace suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega_v\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain with finitely many connected components (the vacuum region of the additional bounded $C^\infty$ ambient branch of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]] by [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]], or any bounded smooth domain), let $\rho$ be continuous on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ (the fixed-time volume source density, C m$^{-3}$ of [[def-em-si-conventions]]), and let $\varphi_1,\varphi_2\in C^2(\overline{\Omega_v})$ be real potentials of the pure electrostatic regime [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with fields $E_i:=-\nabla\varphi_i$ of [[def-em-fields]] and

$$-\Delta\varphi_i=\rho/\varepsilon_0\qquad\text{pointwise on }\Omega_v,\qquad \Delta=\operatorname{div}\nabla.$$

The Laplacian convention is [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. Let $\nu$ denote the outward unit normal of $\Omega_v$ ([[def-classical-normal-derivative]]). Then:

(a) [Classical Dirichlet uniqueness] if $\varphi_1=\varphi_2$ on $\partial\Omega_v$, then $\varphi_1=\varphi_2$ on $\overline{\Omega_v}$, and hence $E_1=E_2$. The conclusion holds component by component; each connected component of a bounded $C^\infty$ domain is again a bounded $C^\infty$ domain, to which the connected-domain uniqueness corollary applies.

(b) [Classical Neumann uniqueness and compatibility] if $\partial_\nu\varphi_1=\partial_\nu\varphi_2$ on $\partial\Omega_v$, then $\varphi_1-\varphi_2$ is constant on each connected component of $\Omega_v$, and conversely adding one real constant per component to a solution preserves both the equation and the Neumann data; hence the field $E$ is unique while the potential is determined only up to componentwise constants. Moreover the Neumann data are necessarily compatible:

$$\int_{\Omega_v^{(j)}}\rho\,dx+\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial\Omega_v^{(j)}}\partial_\nu\varphi\,dS=0\qquad\text{for every connected component }\Omega_v^{(j)}.$$

This compatibility is necessary, not sufficient, and is exactly the flux identity of the divergence theorem for the Poisson equation.

(c) [Weak variants] (i) if $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega_v)$ ([[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]) is prescribed as a trace and $\varphi_1,\varphi_2\in H^1(\Omega_v)$ are weak solutions of the Dirichlet problem with the same trace $g$, then $\varphi_1=\varphi_2$; (ii) if the conormal data are prescribed compatibly, weak $H^1$ solutions are unique modulo constants on each connected component, and for connected $\Omega_v$ this is the normalised solution of [[lem-em-weak-neumann-and-transmission-existence]]; (iii) [sheet/transmission variant] for the finite disjoint smooth interfaces and outer Dirichlet data of [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]](c), the globally $H^1$ solution is unique, and for compatible outer Neumann data it is unique modulo componentwise constants until the componentwise means are fixed.

(d) [Physics reading and conductor case] on a star-shaped vacuum domain the curl-free $C^1$ field has an interior $C^2$ potential by [[pthm-em-electrostatic-potential]]. This alone does not supply closure regularity, $H^1$ membership, a trace, or prescribed boundary data; each application of (a)-(c) additionally requires its stated regularity and identical boundary/source data. In the bounded conductor model, prescribed absolute conductor potentials $V_j$ and absolute outer Dirichlet data determine the potential and field uniquely in the admitted classical or weak class. Grounding fixes the additive constant exactly. If only relative potential differences are prescribed and the outer/reference data are also allowed to shift by the same constant, the common gauge constant is free; merely omitting outer boundary data does not establish field uniqueness.

(e) [Scope] uniqueness is conditional on the stated boundary or decay data: on an unbounded exterior region without a decay condition uniqueness fails: on $\Omega_R=\{x:|x|>R\}$ the functions $0$ and $u(x)=1-R/|x|$ are two distinct bounded harmonic functions with the same zero boundary trace and different limits at infinity, so the boundary, decay and regularity hypotheses above cannot be dropped. No existence is inferred from uniqueness; the classical branch requires $C^2$ up to the closure, the weak branches carry their own domain, coefficient and trace hypotheses, and no dielectric material coefficient or empirical claim is included. For the admitted conductor class with connected vacuum, fixed absolute conductor potentials and identical outer Neumann data also give exact uniqueness: this is a mixed boundary problem with a nonempty Dirichlet part, so there is no surviving additive constant. Existence for those mixed data is not asserted here. In that weak mixed branch, write $\mathcal V_D=\{v\in H^1(\Omega_v):Tv=0\text{ on }\partial D\}$. The compared potentials have the same prescribed conductor trace and satisfy $\varepsilon_0\int_{\Omega_v}\nabla v\cdot\nabla\varphi=\int_{\Omega_v}\rho v+\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,Tv$ for every $v\in\mathcal V_D$, with the same smooth outer normal datum $g$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the cited solvability theorem ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega_v\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] with finitely many connected components (the vacuum region of the additional bounded $C^\infty$ ambient branch of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]] by [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]], or any bounded smooth domain), let $\rho$ be smooth on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ (fixed-time volume source density, C m$^{-3}$ of [[def-em-si-conventions]]) and let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be the framework constant. Then the electrostatic boundary value problems on $\Omega_v$ are solvable in the following exact senses, and the solutions are the fields of the pure electrostatic regime [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with volume source $\rho$:

(a) [Dirichlet branch] for every $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$ there is exactly one $\varphi\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$ with

$$-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0\quad\text{on }\Omega_v,\qquad \varphi|_{\partial\Omega_v}=g,$$

with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]];
and it is the unique weak $H^1$ solution with trace $g$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] for the class); the field $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ ([[def-em-fields]]) is $C^\infty$ on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ and $(E,0)$ realises the pure electrostatic regime with source $\rho$ on the vacuum region.

(b) [Neumann branch] for every $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$ with

$$\int_{\Omega_v^{(j)}}\rho\,dx+\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial\Omega_v^{(j)}}g\,dS=0\qquad\text{for every connected component }\Omega_v^{(j)}\text{ of }\Omega_v,$$

there is $\varphi\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$ with $-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $\partial_\nu\varphi=g$ (outward normal $\nu$, [[def-classical-normal-derivative]]), unique up to one additive constant per connected component; the normalisation $\int_{\Omega_v^{(j)}}\varphi\,dx=0$ for every $j$ selects exactly one. The compatibility is also necessary in the sense of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]](b).

(c) [Conductor reading and surface-charge realization] for the separated compact-body conductor geometry and zero-interior-volume convention of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]], additionally assuming $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^\infty$ ambient domain, with outer boundary data $g_0\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ on $\partial\Omega$ and constants $V_j$ on the conductor surfaces $\partial D_j$ (constant functions are smooth on the compact disjoint boundary pieces), the combined datum is a special case of (a); the field $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\Omega_v$ extended by $E:=0$ on the conductor satisfies the adopted distributional vacuum Maxwell equations [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]] with the source pair $(\rho_v+\sigma\,\delta_{\partial D},\,0)$, where $\sigma:=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot E_+\in C^\infty(\partial D)$ is the constructed continuous surface-charge density, agreeing afterwards with [[pthm-em-conductor-surface-charge]] ([[def-em-weak-sources]](c), [[def-em-surface-distribution]], [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]]); the total charges $Q_j=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}n\cdot E_+\,dS$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]) are thereby determined by the data, and $\varphi$ is constant on each $\partial D_j$ with value $V_j$.

(d) [Stationary sheet charge in the vacuum region] for finitely many disjoint closed smooth interfaces $\Gamma$ strictly inside $\Omega_v$, a smooth sheet density $\sigma_\Gamma$ on them, and outer Dirichlet data $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$, there is a weak solution $\varphi\in H^1(\Omega_v)$ which is $C^\infty$ on the closure of each side of every $\Gamma$, unique by [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]](c)(iii), solving the weak equation with right-hand side $\int_{\Omega_v}\rho v+\sum_\Gamma\int_\Gamma\sigma_\Gamma\,Tv$; its flux jump is $n\cdot[\varepsilon_0\nabla\varphi]=-\sigma_\Gamma$, equivalently $n\cdot[E]=\sigma_\Gamma/\varepsilon_0$ in the sign convention of [[pthm-em-fixed-vacuum-jumps]]. This is the vacuum ($\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0$) transmission branch; no dielectric coefficient is introduced.

(e) [Scope] all existence statements are the ones proved in [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]] for its stated smooth bounded domains, smooth uniformly positive coefficients (here $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0 I$), smooth data and finitely many disjoint smooth interfaces; the coefficient is the smooth positive constant $\varepsilon_0I$ on every side in the transmission clause. Excluded: nonsmooth boundaries, corners, edges, coefficient loss of regularity, prescribed total charges for conductor bodies (the free equipotential problem), unbounded exterior regions without a stated decay class, dielectric material response (belonging to the material-response page) and any measurement, apparatus or empirical claim. The theorem asserts existence of the potential, not of a physical equilibrium; the ideal conductor is the adopted model of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]].

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units, constants and symbols of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and let $(\rho,J)$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$, all of class $C^1$ (with every additional derivative appearing below existing and continuous); $\partial_t$ is the partial time derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

(a) [Static regime] The **static (time-independent) electromagnetic regime** on $\Omega\times I$ is the requirement
$$\partial_tE=0,\qquad\partial_tB=0,\qquad\partial_t\rho=0,\qquad\partial_tJ=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

(b) [Pure electrostatics] The **pure electrostatic regime** is the static regime together with $J=0$ and $B=0$ on $\Omega\times I$.

(c) [Reduced equations] If the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds in the static regime, then the four Maxwell equations reduce to
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$$
pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied at each fixed time; in the pure electrostatic regime the reduction is exactly the pair $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$.

(d) [Fixed-time reading] In the static regime $E,B,\rho,J$ do not depend on $t$, so each is the pullback along $(y,t)\mapsto y$ of a single map on $\Omega$; this fixed-time reading (the spatial field or source) is the object analysed by the electrostatic statements of this page, and no other time dependence is introduced. The equations of (c) are equations between those spatial maps.

(e) [Static-to-distributional reading] Let fields $E,B$ and volume densities $\rho,J$ be locally integrable and time independent on $\Omega\times I$, and let $\Omega$ be open. Then, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the cited measure and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), the weak equations of the solution predicate of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e) for these time-independent objects hold if and only if the four spatial equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$; the passage between them is the integration in $t$ of the pairings against $C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ tests, justified by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] after identifying fields and densities with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). In particular a **stationary point charge** at $x_0\in\Omega$ with charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ is the point source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with constant trajectory $z(t)\equiv x_0$, whose pairing is $\psi\mapsto q\int_I\psi(x_0,t)\,dt$ and whose fixed-time reading is the spatial point source $\eta\mapsto q\eta(x_0)$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).

(f) [Conventions and scope] The regime is imposed in the one inertial frame of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; no claim is made that time independence survives a change of inertial description, and where a frame change is used the transformed fields must be rechecked. The static regime is an adopted idealization, not a dynamical stability theorem: static charged matter requires external support or an adopted equilibrium model. No equation is asserted here for singular sources beyond the dictionary of (e), and no empirical claim is made.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

derivations.claim: Geometry and area of the unit ball: $B$ is a bounded $C^\infty$ domain with $\partial B=S^2$ and outward normal $\nu(x)=x$; it is connected and nonempty. The area is $|S^2|=4\pi$: by $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$ and $V_n(1)=\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2+1)$, the functional equation gives $\Gamma(5/2)=\frac32\Gamma(3/2)=\frac32\cdot\frac12\Gamma(1/2)=\frac{3\sqrt\pi}{4}$ with $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$, so $V_3(1)=\pi^{3/2}/(3\sqrt\pi/4)=4\pi/3$ and $|S^2|=3V_3(1)=4\pi$.

Classical exclusion (a): suppose a real $\varphi\in C^2(\overline B)$ satisfies $-\Delta\varphi=0$ in $B$ and $\partial_
u\varphi=1$ on $\partial B$; put $f:=-\Delta\varphi=0$ and $g:=\partial_
u\varphi\equiv1$. By [F1] applied on the bounded $C^1$ domain $B$ with the outward normal $
u$, $0=\int_B f\,d\lambda_3=-\int_{\partial B}g\,dS=-|S^2|=-4\pi$ by [step 1.1], a contradiction since $4\pi
e0$; hence no such $\varphi$ exists. This is (a), and it exhibits the failure of the necessary compatibility of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]](b).

The datum $g\equiv1$ as an element of the dual trace space: $1\in L^2(S^2)$ by [F6], so for $h\in H^{1/2}(S^2)$ the integral $\int_{S^2}h\,dS$ is absolutely convergent, and Cauchy-Schwarz together with the inclusion bound of [F3] gives $|\int_{S^2}h\,dS|\le|S^2|^{1/2}\|h\|_{L^2(S^2)}\le C|S^2|^{1/2}\|h\|_{H^{1/2}(S^2)}$; hence $g\equiv1$ defines a bounded linear functional $\langle g,\cdot\rangle$ on $H^{1/2}(S^2)$, i.e. an element of $H^{-1/2}(\partial B)$, with $\langle g,h\rangle=\int_{S^2}h\,dS$.

Companion failure with unit source and zero boundary field: for $f\equiv1$ on $B$ and $g\equiv0$ on $\partial B$, any hypothetical $\varphi\in C^2(\overline B)$ with $-\Delta\varphi=f$ and $\partial_
u\varphi=g$ would satisfy, by [F1], $\int_B f\,d\lambda_3=|B_1|=V_3(1)=4\pi/3
e0=-\int_{\partial B}0\,dS$, a contradiction; thus the same flux budget excludes the unit-source datum, and in the weak formulation the corresponding functional $\ell'(v)=\int_B v\,d\lambda_3$ has $\ell'(1)=4\pi/3
e0$, excluding weak solutions by [F4] as well.

The functional $\ell(v):=\langle g,Tv\rangle=\int_{S^2}Tv\,dS$ on $H^1(B)$: it is well defined because $Tv\in L^2(S^2)$ by [F3] and $L^2(S^2)\subset L^1(S^2)$ with $\int_{S^2}|Tv|\,dS\le|S^2|^{1/2}\|Tv\|_{L^2(S^2)}$ by Cauchy-Schwarz and $|S^2|<\infty$ [F5, F6]; it is linear and bounded, $|\ell(v)|\le|S^2|^{1/2}\|Tv\|_{L^2(S^2)}\le C'\|v\|_{H^1(B)}$, by the trace bound [F3]. At the constant function $v\equiv1$ one has $\ell(1)=\int_{S^2}T1\,dS=\int_{S^2}1\,dS=|S^2|=4\pi\ne0$ by [F6] and [step 1.1].

Weak exclusion (b): with $\Omega=B$ (bounded, connected, $C^1$), $\varepsilon=I$ (symmetric, uniformly elliptic), $ho=0\in L^2(B)$ and $g\equiv1\in H^{-1/2}(\partial B)$ from [step 2.2], the data functional of the weak Neumann problem is exactly $\ell$ of [step 3.1]; by the criterion [F4], a weak solution $u\in H^1(B)$ with $\int_B
abla v\cdot
abla u\,d\lambda_3=\ell(v)=\langle g,Tvangle$ for all $v\in H^1(B)$ exists if and only if $\ell(1)=0$, but $\ell(1)=4\pi
e0$ by [step 3.1]; hence no such $u$ exists. The obstruction is already visible by testing $v\equiv1$: the left side vanishes and the right side is $4\pi$. This is (b).

Reading and scope (c): on the unit ball with zero volume source the unit outward normal-derivative datum is inadmissible in both the classical $C^2(\overline B)$ class and the weak $H^1(B)$ class; the obstruction is the strictly positive total boundary flux $|S^2|=4\pi$, not smoothness or compactness, and the necessary compatibility $\int_{\partial B}g\,dS=0$ for the zero-source problem is a flux budget whereas sufficiency in the smooth class is the separate content of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-existence]](b) under its hypotheses [F7]. No step uses the ball's symmetry beyond the area computation of [step 1.1]; no measurement, apparatus or material property is asserted, and the companion failure of [step 2.3] is the same flux obstruction evaluated at $f\equiv1$, $g\equiv0$. This is (c).

risk_review.notes: All seven steps checked. The unit ball is smooth and connected with radial normal. Gamma recurrence at 1/2,3/2 gives volume 4pi/3 and chart/polar area 4pi. Classical compatibility with f=0,g=1 would give 0=−4pi. The fractional trace atlas controls its L2 norm; Cauchy-Schwarz makes g=1 a bounded real dual functional, and the trace agrees with restriction, T1=1. In H1 the constant test is admissible and gives 0=ell(1)=4pi, excluding weak solutions directly as well as through the exact Neumann iff. The companion f=1,g=0 violates compatibility by 4pi/3. All cited supplier interfaces match the explicit AC/AC_omega costs. SI readings distinguish derivative datum 1 V/m from physical density and flux 4pi V m; necessary compatibility alone is not a general sufficiency theorem. Reader's trace-dual justification and unit corrections are retained.

boundaries.evidence: The conductor family has m>=1 bodies and the grounded outer boundary is nonempty ([F1]); the zero datum V=0 is included and treated in steps 2.1/4.1.
Steps 2.1 and 3.1: V=0 gives phi^V=0, Q=0 and U=0. The diagonal capacitance entries are positive; positivity of every off-diagonal entry is neither asserted nor proved.
The case m=1 is the two-terminal reading of clause (d), proved in step 4.1; one vacuum component is the model's connectedness requirement.
The degenerate datum V=0 is handled before dividing by t in step 4.1; no degenerate conductor geometry occurs because the bodies are compact, separated and lie in a bounded smooth ambient branch.
The assembly family endpoints s=0 and s=1 are evaluated in step 4.2 with the integral of s over [0,1] equal to 1/2; the boundary traces used at endpoints are the continuous closure traces of [F2].

Full AC for the unit-Dirichlet solvability interface and AC_omega for the surface and integral interfaces are declared; the linearity, reciprocity and energy computations add no stronger choice (step 1.1).
The vanishing-energy direction U(V)=0 implies V=0 is step 3.1 via almost-everywhere vanishing, continuity, constancy on the connected vacuum and vanishing on the nonempty outer boundary.
The direction V=0 implies U(V)=0 is step 3.1 with step 2.1: phi^0 is the zero potential, so the energy integral vanishes.

citations.quote:
Under the Countable Choice convention of the stated boundary and sheet-distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), adopt as a physical model of ideal electrostatic conductors, for the classical laboratory framework of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]: a **conductor configuration** consists of the following data, and every model of this postulate is required to satisfy the clauses below. No experiment is reported and no empirical value is inferred; this is an explicitly adopted equilibrium idealization together with its geometric and source conventions.

(a) [Geometry] a laboratory region $\Omega\times I$ with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ an arbitrary open ambient region, a finite family $D_1,\dots,D_m$ ($m\ge1$) of bounded $C^\infty$ domains with pairwise disjoint closures in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] with closures strictly inside $\Omega$ (the **conductor bodies**), the **conductor** $D:=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_m$, its **surface** $\partial D$, and the **vacuum region** $\Omega_v:=\Omega\setminus\overline D$. By [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]], $\partial D=\partial D_1\cup\cdots\cup\partial D_m$ is a disjoint union of compact embedded $C^\infty$ hypersurfaces. The vacuum $\Omega_v$ is open, and near each conductor surface it is locally the smooth exterior side of that conductor. No boundedness or regularity of the ambient boundary is inferred from openness. In the additional **bounded smooth ambient branch**, assume that $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^\infty$ domain; only then [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]] gives that $\Omega_v$ is a bounded $C^\infty$ domain with the specified outer/conductor boundary charts; we additionally require $\Omega_v$ to be connected (configurations whose vacuum region is separated by the conductors, for instance by an enclosing closed shell, are outside this model as formulated here).

(b) [Equilibrium and sources] the configuration is in the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] on the vacuum region: $B=0$, $J=0$, $E$ is the fixed-time electric field of [[def-em-fields]], the volume source density $\rho_v$ is a continuous real map on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ (C m$^{-3}$, [[def-em-sources]]) extended by zero to $D$; the **conductor charge is a stationary surface charge**, i.e. a continuous density $\sigma:\partial D\to\mathbb R$ (C m$^{-2}$) whose pairing with test functions is the stationary-sheet source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) with tangential current $K=0$ and $S=\partial D$; and the field pair $(E,0)$ together with the source pair $(\rho_v+\sigma\,\delta_{\partial D},\ 0)$ satisfies the adopted distributional vacuum Maxwell equations [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]]. Inside the conductor the field vanishes: $E\equiv0$ on $D$ (the **equilibrium condition**); equivalently the conductor interior is field-free and carries no volume charge.

(c) [Potential and equipotential convention] there is a function $\varphi\in C^0(\Omega)\cap C^2(\Omega_v)$ with $E=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\Omega_v$ and with $\varphi$ constant on each conductor body, $\varphi|_{D_j}\equiv V_j$ for real constants $V_j$ (volts, [[def-em-si-conventions]]); by continuity of $\varphi$ the trace of $\varphi$ on each $\partial D_j$ from the vacuum side equals $V_j$ as well. This is the single-function convention of an ideal conductor with no double layer: the model reads the same potential value on both sides of $\partial D_j$, while the normal component of $E$ may jump.

(d) [Data] a model is completed either by the component potentials $V_1,\dots,V_m$ together with the volume source $\rho_v$ and the data on $\partial\Omega$ where the laboratory region is bounded, or by the component total charges $Q_j:=\int_{\partial D_j}\sigma\,dS$ (C) together with those same ambient data. These are two declared data types; the postulate asserts neither that both data types are simultaneously specifiable nor that either is solvable for arbitrary data.

(e) [Scope] This is a static, frame-relative equilibrium idealization: it excludes transient finite-conductivity dynamics, relaxation to equilibrium, moving surface charge, electrode polarization and contact effects, and it is not derived from a microscopic matter model. It asserts no existence or uniqueness theorem (those are separate conditional results), no force, no energy, no radiation, no measurement and no apparatus realization; the value $V_j$ is a model parameter and the surface density $\sigma$ is an idealization variable determined by the equilibrium problem when it is solvable. The general open ambient branch retains compact conductor bodies in exterior configurations. Its additional bounded smooth ambient branch is distinct from the separately declared grounded-half-space and infinite parallel-plane idealizations, whose conductor bodies are themselves noncompact. Those examples retain the equilibrium/equipotential interpretation but their noncompact bodies and plane distributions are not instances of this compact-body configuration or its compact-sheet predicate. No arbitrary exterior solvability is asserted.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units, constants and symbols of [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be fields of [[def-em-fields]] and let $(\rho,J)$ be source fields of [[def-em-sources]] on $\Omega\times I$, all of class $C^1$ (with every additional derivative appearing below existing and continuous); $\partial_t$ is the partial time derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

(a) [Static regime] The **static (time-independent) electromagnetic regime** on $\Omega\times I$ is the requirement
$$\partial_tE=0,\qquad\partial_tB=0,\qquad\partial_t\rho=0,\qquad\partial_tJ=0\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$

(b) [Pure electrostatics] The **pure electrostatic regime** is the static regime together with $J=0$ and $B=0$ on $\Omega\times I$.

(c) [Reduced equations] If the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds in the static regime, then the four Maxwell equations reduce to
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$$
pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, with $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied at each fixed time; in the pure electrostatic regime the reduction is exactly the pair $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$.

(d) [Fixed-time reading] In the static regime $E,B,\rho,J$ do not depend on $t$, so each is the pullback along $(y,t)\mapsto y$ of a single map on $\Omega$; this fixed-time reading (the spatial field or source) is the object analysed by the electrostatic statements of this page, and no other time dependence is introduced. The equations of (c) are equations between those spatial maps.

(e) [Static-to-distributional reading] Let fields $E,B$ and volume densities $\rho,J$ be locally integrable and time independent on $\Omega\times I$, and let $\Omega$ be open. Then, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of the cited measure and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]), the weak equations of the solution predicate of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e) for these time-independent objects hold if and only if the four spatial equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$; the passage between them is the integration in $t$ of the pairings against $C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ tests, justified by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] after identifying fields and densities with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). In particular a **stationary point charge** at $x_0\in\Omega$ with charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ is the point source of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with constant trajectory $z(t)\equiv x_0$, whose pairing is $\psi\mapsto q\int_I\psi(x_0,t)\,dt$ and whose fixed-time reading is the spatial point source $\eta\mapsto q\eta(x_0)$ ([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).

(f) [Conventions and scope] The regime is imposed in the one inertial frame of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; no claim is made that time independence survives a change of inertial description, and where a frame change is used the transformed fields must be rechecked. The static regime is an adopted idealization, not a dynamical stability theorem: static charged matter requires external support or an adopted equilibrium model. No equation is asserted here for singular sources beyond the dictionary of (e), and no empirical claim is made.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the cited solvability theorem ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega_v\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain in the sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] with finitely many connected components (the vacuum region of the additional bounded $C^\infty$ ambient branch of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]] by [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]], or any bounded smooth domain), let $\rho$ be smooth on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ (fixed-time volume source density, C m$^{-3}$ of [[def-em-si-conventions]]) and let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be the framework constant. Then the electrostatic boundary value problems on $\Omega_v$ are solvable in the following exact senses, and the solutions are the fields of the pure electrostatic regime [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with volume source $\rho$:

(a) [Dirichlet branch] for every $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$ there is exactly one $\varphi\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$ with

$$-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0\quad\text{on }\Omega_v,\qquad \varphi|_{\partial\Omega_v}=g,$$

with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]];
and it is the unique weak $H^1$ solution with trace $g$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] for the class); the field $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ ([[def-em-fields]]) is $C^\infty$ on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ and $(E,0)$ realises the pure electrostatic regime with source $\rho$ on the vacuum region.

(b) [Neumann branch] for every $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$ with

$$\int_{\Omega_v^{(j)}}\rho\,dx+\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial\Omega_v^{(j)}}g\,dS=0\qquad\text{for every connected component }\Omega_v^{(j)}\text{ of }\Omega_v,$$

there is $\varphi\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$ with $-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $\partial_\nu\varphi=g$ (outward normal $\nu$, [[def-classical-normal-derivative]]), unique up to one additive constant per connected component; the normalisation $\int_{\Omega_v^{(j)}}\varphi\,dx=0$ for every $j$ selects exactly one. The compatibility is also necessary in the sense of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]](b).

(c) [Conductor reading and surface-charge realization] for the separated compact-body conductor geometry and zero-interior-volume convention of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]], additionally assuming $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^\infty$ ambient domain, with outer boundary data $g_0\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ on $\partial\Omega$ and constants $V_j$ on the conductor surfaces $\partial D_j$ (constant functions are smooth on the compact disjoint boundary pieces), the combined datum is a special case of (a); the field $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\Omega_v$ extended by $E:=0$ on the conductor satisfies the adopted distributional vacuum Maxwell equations [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]] with the source pair $(\rho_v+\sigma\,\delta_{\partial D},\,0)$, where $\sigma:=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot E_+\in C^\infty(\partial D)$ is the constructed continuous surface-charge density, agreeing afterwards with [[pthm-em-conductor-surface-charge]] ([[def-em-weak-sources]](c), [[def-em-surface-distribution]], [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]]); the total charges $Q_j=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}n\cdot E_+\,dS$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]) are thereby determined by the data, and $\varphi$ is constant on each $\partial D_j$ with value $V_j$.

(d) [Stationary sheet charge in the vacuum region] for finitely many disjoint closed smooth interfaces $\Gamma$ strictly inside $\Omega_v$, a smooth sheet density $\sigma_\Gamma$ on them, and outer Dirichlet data $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$, there is a weak solution $\varphi\in H^1(\Omega_v)$ which is $C^\infty$ on the closure of each side of every $\Gamma$, unique by [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]](c)(iii), solving the weak equation with right-hand side $\int_{\Omega_v}\rho v+\sum_\Gamma\int_\Gamma\sigma_\Gamma\,Tv$; its flux jump is $n\cdot[\varepsilon_0\nabla\varphi]=-\sigma_\Gamma$, equivalently $n\cdot[E]=\sigma_\Gamma/\varepsilon_0$ in the sign convention of [[pthm-em-fixed-vacuum-jumps]]. This is the vacuum ($\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0$) transmission branch; no dielectric coefficient is introduced.

(e) [Scope] all existence statements are the ones proved in [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]] for its stated smooth bounded domains, smooth uniformly positive coefficients (here $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0 I$), smooth data and finitely many disjoint smooth interfaces; the coefficient is the smooth positive constant $\varepsilon_0I$ on every side in the transmission clause. Excluded: nonsmooth boundaries, corners, edges, coefficient loss of regularity, prescribed total charges for conductor bodies (the free equipotential problem), unbounded exterior regions without a stated decay class, dielectric material response (belonging to the material-response page) and any measurement, apparatus or empirical claim. The theorem asserts existence of the potential, not of a physical equilibrium; the ideal conductor is the adopted model of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the cited weak-solvability and trace suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega_v\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain with finitely many connected components (the vacuum region of the additional bounded $C^\infty$ ambient branch of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]] by [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]], or any bounded smooth domain), let $\rho$ be continuous on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ (the fixed-time volume source density, C m$^{-3}$ of [[def-em-si-conventions]]), and let $\varphi_1,\varphi_2\in C^2(\overline{\Omega_v})$ be real potentials of the pure electrostatic regime [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with fields $E_i:=-\nabla\varphi_i$ of [[def-em-fields]] and

$$-\Delta\varphi_i=\rho/\varepsilon_0\qquad\text{pointwise on }\Omega_v,\qquad \Delta=\operatorname{div}\nabla.$$

The Laplacian convention is [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. Let $\nu$ denote the outward unit normal of $\Omega_v$ ([[def-classical-normal-derivative]]). Then:

(a) [Classical Dirichlet uniqueness] if $\varphi_1=\varphi_2$ on $\partial\Omega_v$, then $\varphi_1=\varphi_2$ on $\overline{\Omega_v}$, and hence $E_1=E_2$. The conclusion holds component by component; each connected component of a bounded $C^\infty$ domain is again a bounded $C^\infty$ domain, to which the connected-domain uniqueness corollary applies.

(b) [Classical Neumann uniqueness and compatibility] if $\partial_\nu\varphi_1=\partial_\nu\varphi_2$ on $\partial\Omega_v$, then $\varphi_1-\varphi_2$ is constant on each connected component of $\Omega_v$, and conversely adding one real constant per component to a solution preserves both the equation and the Neumann data; hence the field $E$ is unique while the potential is determined only up to componentwise constants. Moreover the Neumann data are necessarily compatible:

$$\int_{\Omega_v^{(j)}}\rho\,dx+\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial\Omega_v^{(j)}}\partial_\nu\varphi\,dS=0\qquad\text{for every connected component }\Omega_v^{(j)}.$$

This compatibility is necessary, not sufficient, and is exactly the flux identity of the divergence theorem for the Poisson equation.

(c) [Weak variants] (i) if $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega_v)$ ([[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]) is prescribed as a trace and $\varphi_1,\varphi_2\in H^1(\Omega_v)$ are weak solutions of the Dirichlet problem with the same trace $g$, then $\varphi_1=\varphi_2$; (ii) if the conormal data are prescribed compatibly, weak $H^1$ solutions are unique modulo constants on each connected component, and for connected $\Omega_v$ this is the normalised solution of [[lem-em-weak-neumann-and-transmission-existence]]; (iii) [sheet/transmission variant] for the finite disjoint smooth interfaces and outer Dirichlet data of [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]](c), the globally $H^1$ solution is unique, and for compatible outer Neumann data it is unique modulo componentwise constants until the componentwise means are fixed.

(d) [Physics reading and conductor case] on a star-shaped vacuum domain the curl-free $C^1$ field has an interior $C^2$ potential by [[pthm-em-electrostatic-potential]]. This alone does not supply closure regularity, $H^1$ membership, a trace, or prescribed boundary data; each application of (a)-(c) additionally requires its stated regularity and identical boundary/source data. In the bounded conductor model, prescribed absolute conductor potentials $V_j$ and absolute outer Dirichlet data determine the potential and field uniquely in the admitted classical or weak class. Grounding fixes the additive constant exactly. If only relative potential differences are prescribed and the outer/reference data are also allowed to shift by the same constant, the common gauge constant is free; merely omitting outer boundary data does not establish field uniqueness.

(e) [Scope] uniqueness is conditional on the stated boundary or decay data: on an unbounded exterior region without a decay condition uniqueness fails: on $\Omega_R=\{x:|x|>R\}$ the functions $0$ and $u(x)=1-R/|x|$ are two distinct bounded harmonic functions with the same zero boundary trace and different limits at infinity, so the boundary, decay and regularity hypotheses above cannot be dropped. No existence is inferred from uniqueness; the classical branch requires $C^2$ up to the closure, the weak branches carry their own domain, coefficient and trace hypotheses, and no dielectric material coefficient or empirical claim is included. For the admitted conductor class with connected vacuum, fixed absolute conductor potentials and identical outer Neumann data also give exact uniqueness: this is a mixed boundary problem with a nonempty Dirichlet part, so there is no surviving additive constant. Existence for those mixed data is not asserted here. In that weak mixed branch, write $\mathcal V_D=\{v\in H^1(\Omega_v):Tv=0\text{ on }\partial D\}$. The compared potentials have the same prescribed conductor trace and satisfy $\varepsilon_0\int_{\Omega_v}\nabla v\cdot\nabla\varphi=\int_{\Omega_v}\rho v+\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,Tv$ for every $v\in\mathcal V_D$, with the same smooth outer normal datum $g$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) inherited from the surface and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(\Omega;D_1,\dots,D_m;\Omega_v;E;\rho_v;\sigma;V_j)$ be a model of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]] with surface $S:=\partial D$ and vacuum region $\Omega_v$, with the fields of [[def-em-fields]], the constants and units of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] carried by the model, and suppose additionally that the field $E$ satisfies the joint one-sided $C^1$ regularity hypothesis of [[pthm-em-fixed-vacuum-jumps]] across $S$: around every $x_0\in S$ each side of $S$ is the restriction of a $C^1$ field on an open neighbourhood of the corresponding closed side of a smaller graph chart. Let $n$ denote the unit normal on $S$ pointing from the conductor side into the vacuum side (equivalently: $n$ is the inward normal of $\Omega_v$ and the outward normal of $D$ on $S$, by the local exterior conductor chart; in the bounded smooth ambient branch this is the sign convention of [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]](c)), and let $E_+$ denote the vacuum-side trace of $E$ (the field is zero on the conductor side, so $[E]=E_+$). Then, pointwise on $S$:

(a) [Normal sheet charge] $n\cdot E_+=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ and $n\times E_+=0$; equivalently $\sigma=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot E_+$ and the tangential part of the vacuum-side field vanishes: $E_+$ has no component tangent to $S$. In particular a conductor surface with $\sigma=0$ at a point has $E_+=0$ there (both traces vanish), and the sign of $\sigma$ is the sign of the outward normal field component.

(b) [Normal derivative of the potential] with $\varphi$ the model's potential and $\partial\varphi/\partial n:=\nabla\varphi_+\cdot n$ the one-sided normal derivative in the direction $n$ from the conductor into the vacuum ([[def-classical-normal-derivative]]), one has

$$\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial n}=-\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \sigma=-\varepsilon_0\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial n}.$$

(c) [Equipotential boundary traces] the trace $\varphi_+$ of $\varphi$ on $S$ is constant on each connected component of $S$, with value $V_j$ on every connected component contained in $\partial D_j$; consequently the boundary value problem in the vacuum region is a Dirichlet problem whose data are the constants $V_j$ on the conductor surfaces.

(d) [Total charges] the total charge of conductor $j$ is

$$Q_j=\int_{\partial D_j}\sigma\,dS=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}n\cdot E_+\,dS=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\nu}\,dS,$$

where $\nu$ is the local outward normal of the vacuum along the smooth conductor interface $S$, without asserting regularity of a general ambient outer boundary (so $\nu=-n$ on $\partial D$ and the last equality uses $\partial\varphi/\partial\nu=-\partial\varphi/\partial n$); the surface integrals exist as integrals of continuous functions over the compact embedded hypersurfaces $\partial D_j$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-em-boundary-of-a-bounded-smooth-domain-is-a-compact-embedded-hypersurface]]).

(e) [Data reading] the two data types of the model are related through (d): if the component potentials and ambient data are fixed and the equilibrium solution is given, the total charges are determined by (d); prescribing the total charges instead determines the potentials only through the (separate) equilibrium problem, and this theorem asserts no existence or uniqueness for charge data.

(f) [Scope] The statement is pointwise and stationary: it assumes the one-sided joint regularity above, a $C^\infty$ conductor surface, and the pure electrostatic regime; it excludes moving surface charge, normal sheet currents, magnetic sheet sources, nonsmooth or cornered conductors, fields without one-sided traces, forces, energy and any measurement; no self-force or material response is asserted.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

For a bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega$ and $u\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, the classical normal derivative is $\partial_
u u(x)=Du(x)\cdot
u(x)$ on $\partial\Omega$. Here Du is the continuous extension of the interior gradient and $
u$ is the outward unit normal. For a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation define the same expression on each face off its edge set E; arbitrary values on E do not change a surface integral. This definition uses a classical continuous trace, and asserts neither a Sobolev trace nor a conormal derivative.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a bounded $C^1$ domain or have the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation. For real $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ and $v\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$, $$\int_\Omega(v\Delta u+Du\cdot Dv)\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}v\partial_\nu u\,dS.$$ In the piecewise case the right side is the sum over faces, counted once off E. All integrals are finite.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be nonempty, open, and connected, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be totally differentiable at every point ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]). Then $Df=0$ on $U$ if and only if $f$ is constant on $U$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, and let $\gamma:[a,b]\to U$ be piecewise-$C^1$. Then

$$\int_\gamma\nabla\phi\cdot d\mathbf r=\phi(\gamma(b))-\phi(\gamma(a)).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim:
Setup and well-definedness: by [F1] the vacuum region $\Omega_v$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain (indeed $C^\infty$), connected, nonempty, with boundary the disjoint union of the nonempty compact pieces $\partial\Omega,\partial D_1,\dots,\partial D_m$, and with $\partial\Omega$ nonempty. By [F2] each unit-potential solution $\varphi_j\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$ exists and is unique with $-\Delta\varphi_j=0$ and $\varphi_j|_{\partial D_k}=\delta_{jk}$, $\varphi_j|_{\partial\Omega}=0$. The normal $
u$ is the outward unit normal of $\Omega_v$; it points into the conductor on each $\partial D_j$ [F1]. Each flux $\int_{\partial D_j}\partial\varphi_k/\partial
u\,dS$ exists because $\partial\varphi_k/\partial
u$ is continuous on the compact embedded hypersurface $\partial D_j$ carrying finite surface measure [F3], so $C_{jk}$ is well defined.

Linearity and the charge-potential map (a): fix $V\in\mathbb R^m$ and put $\varphi^V:=\sum_{j=1}^mV_j\varphi_j\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$. By linearity of the Laplacian, $-\Delta\varphi^V=\sum_jV_j(-\Delta\varphi_j)=0$ on $\Omega_v$; on $\partial D_k$ one has $\varphi^V=\sum_jV_j\delta_{jk}=V_k$, and on $\partial\Omega$, $\varphi^V=0$. By the uniqueness clause of [F2], $\varphi^V$ is the unique equilibrium potential with conductor potentials $V$ and grounded outer boundary, and the solution is linear in $V$ by construction. Its charges are given by [F3] and the definition of $C$: for each $j$, $Q_j(V)=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}\partial\varphi^V/\partial\nu\,dS=\varepsilon_0\sum_{k=1}^mV_k\int_{\partial D_j}\partial\varphi_k/\partial\nu\,dS=\sum_{k=1}^mC_{jk}V_k$, that is $Q=CV$.

Reciprocity (b): apply Green's first identity [F4] on the bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega_v$ twice, first with $u=\varphi_j$, $v=\varphi_k$ and then with $u=\varphi_k$, $v=\varphi_j$; both functions lie in $C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$ and $\Delta\varphi_j=\Delta\varphi_k=0$, so subtracting the two identities gives $0=\int_{\partial\Omega_v}(\varphi_j\,\partial_
u\varphi_k-\varphi_k\,\partial_
u\varphi_j)\,dS$. The boundary splits into $\partial\Omega$ and the conductor surfaces [F4]; on $\partial\Omega$ both traces of $\varphi_j,\varphi_k$ vanish, so the outer piece contributes $0$, while on $\partial D_\ell$ the traces are $\delta_{j\ell}$ and $\delta_{k\ell}$, so the total reduces to $\int_{\partial D_j}\partial_
u\varphi_k\,dS-\int_{\partial D_k}\partial_
u\varphi_j\,dS$. Multiplying by $\varepsilon_0$ gives $C_{jk}=C_{kj}$ for all $j,k$; the symmetry is exactly Green's antisymmetric pairing of the two harmonic potentials.

Energy identity and positivity (c): apply Green's first identity [F4] once more with $u=v=\varphi^V$: $\int_{\Omega_v}(\varphi^V\Delta\varphi^V+|
abla\varphi^V|^2)\,d\lambda_3=\int_{\partial\Omega_v}\varphi^V\partial_
u\varphi^V\,dS$. The Laplacian term vanishes by [step 2.1], the outer boundary contributes $0$ because $\varphi^V$ vanishes on $\partial\Omega$, and on $\partial D_j$ the trace of $\varphi^V$ is the constant $V_j$, so $\int_{\partial\Omega_v}\varphi^V\partial_
u\varphi^V\,dS=\sum_{j=1}^mV_j\int_{\partial D_j}\partial_
u\varphi^V\,dS$. By [F3] and [step 2.1] this equals $\sum_jV_jQ_j(V)/\varepsilon_0= rac1{\varepsilon_0}\sum_{j,k}V_jC_{jk}V_k= rac1{\varepsilon_0}V^{T}CV$; multiplying by $\varepsilon_0/2$ gives the identity $U(V)= rac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\Omega_v}|
abla\varphi^V|^2\,d\lambda_3= rac12V^{T}CV= rac12\sum_jV_jQ_j(V)$. The energy is nonnegative because the integrand is; if $U(V)=0$, then $\int_{\Omega_v}|
abla\varphi^V|^2\,d\lambda_3=0$, so $|
abla\varphi^V|^2=0$ almost everywhere by [F5], hence everywhere by continuity on the connected open $\Omega_v$ [F5]; thus $\varphi^V$ is constant on $\Omega_v$ by [F5], and the constant is $0$ because $\varphi^V=0$ on the nonempty boundary piece $\partial\Omega$ and $\varphi^V$ is continuous on the closure [F5]; consequently $V_j=\varphi^V|_{\partial D_j}=0$ for every $j$, i.e. $V=0$. Hence $U(V)\ge0$ with equality exactly at $V=0$, and since $C$ is symmetric by [step 2.2], the symmetric bilinear form $V\mapsto rac12V^{T}CV$ is positive definite.

One driven terminal (d): take $V=te_1$ with $t\in\mathbb R$. By [step 2.1], $\varphi^V=t\varphi_1$, $Q_1=C_{11}t$ and $Q_j=C_{j1}t$ for $j\ne1$; by [step 3.1], $U=\frac12C_{11}t^2=\frac12Q_1V_1$. For $t=0$ all charges and the energy vanish while the unit flux defining $C_{11}$ is unchanged; for $t\ne0$ one may divide by $t=V_1$ to obtain $C_{11}=Q_1/V_1$ and $U=Q_1^2/(2C_{11})$, using $C_{11}>0$ from the positive definiteness of [step 3.1] (take $V=e_1$: $U(e_1)=\frac12C_{11}>0$). Hence $C_{11}$ is the positive geometric capacitance of conductor $1$ with respect to the grounded reference, and the displayed identities $U=\frac12QV=Q^2/(2C)=\frac12CV^2$ hold with $C=C_{11}$, $Q=Q_1$, $V=V_1$.

Assembly reading (e): for $0\le s\le1$ put $V(s):=sV$, $\varphi_s:=\varphi^{sV}=s\varphi^V$ by [step 2.1], and $Q_j(s):=Q_j(sV)=sQ_j(V)$, so that $dQ_j(s)=Q_j(V)\,ds$. The prescribed quasistatic external charge-transfer work is $dW_{\rm ext}=\sum_jV_j(s)\,dQ_j(s)=\sum_j(sV_j)Q_j(V)\,ds=s\,ds\sum_jV_jQ_j(V)$, and summing over the conductors and integrating over $s\in[0,1]$ gives $W_{\rm ext}=\bigl(\int_0^1s\,ds\bigr)\sum_jV_jQ_j(V)=\frac12\sum_jV_jQ_j(V)=U$ by [F6] and [step 3.1]. The family is an accounting prescription on the fixed geometry with grounded reference: the potentials vary during assembly, only the final potentials and geometry are fixed, and the sheet-charge accounting is derived directly rather than from the volume-source theorem [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]]; the path-work identity of [F6] gives the endpoint potential-drop reading along any interior piecewise $C^1$ path, with boundary endpoints understood as limits of the continuous closure traces. This is (e).

Scope (f): the theorem used the compact separated conductor geometry and bounded smooth ambient branch with connected vacuum region [F1], the grounded outer boundary, the zero volume source, and the existence and uniqueness of the unit-potential Dirichlet solutions [F2]; the existence theorem was applied only to the constant data $V$ and $0$, so no solvability for arbitrary boundary data or for prescribed total charges is asserted, and no dielectric coefficient, material response, finite-conductivity or transient charging dynamics, radiation, measurement or apparatus claim enters [F1, F2]. The matrix $C$ is a geometric object of the ideal electrostatic model of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]], and the infinite parallel-plane example is a separate idealization outside this bounded geometry; this completes (f) and the theorem.

risk_review.notes: All seven steps checked. The unit Dirichlet data are smooth on disjoint compact boundary pieces, and the bounded connected vacuum with grounded nonempty outer boundary supplies exact solvability and fixes the common gauge. Finite linear combinations are harmonic with the required traces; uniqueness and the vacuum outward-normal flux formula give Q=CV. Two Green identities reduce the reciprocal pairing to Cjk=Ckj. Green with u=v gives epsilon0 integral |grad phi|^2=V^T CV. A zero integral forces zero continuous gradient by positive measure of Euclidean balls; connectedness forces a constant and the grounded boundary forces zero, hence V=0 and strict positive definiteness. The t=0 case does not divide by voltage, while t!=0 gives Q1/V1=C11; each diagonal entry is positive. One driven conductor may coexist with many grounded bodies, so the reader's renamed clause is exact. The s-scaling work integrates s to 1/2 under an explicit accounting prescription, without invoking volume-source energy for singular sheets or claiming a dynamic charging solution. Farad entries use numerical unit-volt normalization. Infinite planes are excluded from this geometry and retained in their separate example. AC and AC_omega supplier assumptions are explicit; no measured inputs or empirical conclusions enter.

All divisors are nonzero: epsilon0>0 by the SI definition, d>0 and area A>0 by hypothesis, and sigma>0 gives V=sigma*d/epsilon0>0. Thus Q/V is defined. The outside-slab field is zero and its pairings vanish; sigma=0 is excluded as an admitted datum.
